We propose a computational approach combining reinforcement learning (RL) agents with multi-scale physiological modeling to simulate patient responses, clinical workflow interactions, and educator feedback systems. The platform will integrate natural language processing for real-time analysis of learner-clinical instructor dialogues and computer vision techniques for procedural skill assessment. HPC resources will enable parallel training of multiple RL agents across diverse clinical specialties (emergency medicine, surgery, critical care) while maintaining the fidelity required for educational validity. Expected outcomes include a framework for quantifying clinical reasoning development through interpretable AI metrics, predictive models of competency trajectory across training phases, and evidence-based guidelines for AI-mediated scenario personalization. This work addresses a critical gap in health professions education by creating scalable, data-driven tools that enhance clinical decision-making training without compromising patient care standards. The computational infrastructure will support validation studies comparing AI-generated simulations with traditional methods across six clinical disciplines, ultimately advancing our understanding of how adaptive technologies can transform competency assessment and curriculum design in health professions education.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on education and administration leadership skills for clinical educators across health professions and specialties. Includes instruction in academic leadership, assessment, clinical decision making, curriculum development, ethics, primary care education, program evaluation, research methods, and statistics.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing decentralized, self-organizing networks for dynamic environmental monitoring in underserved rural regions. Traditional network protocols struggle to maintain reliability and low latency in such environments due to rapidly changing physical conditions, intermittent power availability, and heterogeneous device capabilities. The research proposes a novel computational framework inspired by adaptive biological systems, integrating swarm intelligence algorithms with lightweight machine learning models to enable networks to autonomously reconfigure topology, routing paths, and resource allocation in response to environmental perturbations. The core innovation lies in developing multi-agent simulations that model network nodes as autonomous entities capable of collective decision-making through localized data exchange, prioritizing energy efficiency and fault tolerance without centralized coordination. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will be critical for simulating large-scale networks (10,000+ nodes) under diverse environmental stress scenarios, including stochastic weather patterns, electromagnetic interference, and partial node failures. Computational methods will combine discrete-event network simulations with evolutionary optimization techniques, requiring parallel processing to evaluate millions of configuration permutations. Expected outcomes include 1) a publicly available benchmark dataset quantifying network resilience metrics under real-world constraints, 2) adaptive protocol designs that reduce energy consumption by 30-50% compared to existing mesh networking standards, and 3) predictive models for optimal node placement in terrain-aware deployments. This work bridges gaps between distributed computing, environmental sensing, and complex systems theory, with potential applications in disaster response networks, precision agriculture telemetry, and IoT infrastructure for climate-vulnerable regions. Results will be disseminated through open-source toolkits to support replicable research in emerging fields of ecological networking.
cip_title: Computer Systems Networking and Telecommunications, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in computer systems networking and telecommunications, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of cross-regional communication and ideological exchange in 19th-century Latin America by analyzing large-scale archival datasets, including digitized newspapers, personal correspondence, and government records from Mexico to Argentina. The central research problem lies in tracing how political ideas—such as liberalism, federalism, and anti-colonialism—circulated among urban centers and rural areas during post-independence state formation. Traditional historiographical methods struggle to systematically map these flows across multilingual sources (Spanish, Portuguese, and Indigenous languages) or quantify their impact on regional governance structures. To address this, we propose a computational approach leveraging natural language processing (NLP) and network analysis. Custom transformer models will be trained to detect ideological concepts, semantic shifts, and multilingual terminology in over 500,000 pages of text, while temporal graph algorithms will model the diffusion of ideas through geographic and social networks. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for processing heterogeneous, noisy historical data at scale, particularly for parallelized OCR correction of degraded documents, training multilingual NLP pipelines, and running iterative simulations of network propagation. The project will utilize GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning tasks and high-memory CPUs for constructing dynamic networks with temporal edge weighting. Expected outcomes include an open-access database of annotated texts, interactive visualizations of idea circulation patterns, and quantitative metrics assessing the influence of key cities as ideological hubs. By integrating computational methods with archival research, this work aims to reveal previously obscured connections between intellectual movements and institutional changes, offering new frameworks for understanding the contested construction of national identities in postcolonial Latin America.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history of the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking areas of the world, including the Iberian, Latin American, and Lusophone worlds.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of cultural narratives and identity formation within Canadian Indigenous and immigrant communities through large-scale textual and visual data. Focusing on understudied pre-federation and 20th-century archival materials—including digitized oral histories, multilingual newspapers, and community artwork—the research addresses a critical gap in understanding how intersecting cultural, ethnic, and gender identities have been negotiated in Canada’s pluralistic landscape. Traditional humanities methods struggle to process the scale and complexity of these multimodal datasets, which span over 10 terabytes and include unstructured text in English, French, and Indigenous languages, as well as high-resolution image scans. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) models fine-tuned for historical dialects, computer vision techniques for pattern recognition in visual artifacts, and network analysis to map cross-community influences. Custom pipelines will be developed to handle non-Latin scripts and low-resource languages, while privacy-preserving federated learning protocols will ensure ethical handling of sensitive Indigenous materials. By parallelizing workflows across GPU nodes, the project aims to identify longitudinal trends in cultural self-representation, trace the diffusion of narrative motifs across demographic groups, and quantify shifts in gendered symbolism post-1960s multiculturalism policies. Expected outcomes include the first longitudinal dataset of Canadian intercultural discourse dynamics, open-source tools for heritage language NLP, and visualizations of identity negotiation processes at unprecedented temporal and spatial resolutions. These results will directly inform curricula in Canadian cultural studies and provide evidence-based frameworks for contemporary policy discussions on cultural preservation and inclusive nation-building. The scale of data processing—requiring weeks of sustained computation for transformer model training and hyperparameter optimization—necessitates dedicated HPC allocation to achieve research objectives within feasible timelines.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of Canada and its Pre-Columbian, colonial, and pre-federation predecessors, including immigrant flows and related borderlands and island groups.

abstract: The integration of heterogeneous, high-dimensional health data into actionable insights remains a critical challenge in health information management, particularly as electronic health records (EHRs) expand to include multi-omics, imaging, and real-time sensor data. Current systems struggle to harmonize these disparate data types while preserving patient privacy and enabling scalable analysis. This project proposes the development of a privacy-preserving, machine learning-driven framework to synthesize and analyze multimodal health data, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to overcome computational bottlenecks. The research will focus on creating a federated analytics pipeline that operates across decentralized EHR datasets without raw data exchange, utilizing secure multi-party computation (sMPC) and differential privacy. Key computational tasks include training deep learning models for synthetic data generation that mirror statistical properties of sensitive patient records, optimizing graph-based algorithms to map patient trajectory correlations across modalities, and simulating large-scale data fusion scenarios to stress-test interoperability standards. The HPC environment will enable parallel processing of petabyte-scale datasets, hyperparameter optimization for privacy-utility trade-offs, and validation of synthetic data fidelity through downstream predictive modeling tasks (e.g., early sepsis detection, readmission risk stratification). Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for health systems to safely share synthetic derivatives of protected health information (PHI), novel metrics for quantifying re-identification risks in multimodal health data, and benchmark performance data for distributed learning architectures in HIPAA-compliant environments. This work directly addresses the growing need for advanced computing infrastructure in health information administration, where traditional methods fail to keep pace with the volume and complexity of modern medical data. By enabling secure, large-scale collaboration across institutions, the project aims to accelerate translational research while maintaining rigorous ethical standards for data stewardship—a crucial advancement for precision medicine initiatives reliant on diverse, representative health datasets.
cip_title: Health Information/ Medical Records Administration/ Administrator
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to plan, design, and manage systems, processes, and facilities used to collect, store, secure, retrieve, analyze, and transmit medical records and other health information used by clinical professionals and health care organizations. Includes instruction in the principles and basic content of the biomedical and clinical sciences, information technology and applications, data and database management, clinical research methodologies, health information resources and systems, office management, legal requirements, and professional standards.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework for analyzing systemic financial risk propagation in multi-layered market networks, integrating heterogenous data from derivatives, credit markets, and shadow banking activities. Traditional risk management models struggle to capture the nonlinear interdependencies between regulated financial institutions and less transparent sectors, particularly during stress events where liquidity constraints and collateral calls create cascading failures. The proposed work addresses this gap by constructing dynamic network models that simulate cross-sector risk transmission pathways under varying macroeconomic scenarios, incorporating machine learning-calibrated agent behaviors and regulatory boundary conditions. The computational approach combines graph neural networks with Monte Carlo stress testing, requiring high-performance computing resources to handle three critical challenges: (1) processing real-time streaming data from disparate financial subsystems at scale, (2) resolving complex network interdependencies through iterative graph convolutions, and (3) running ensemble simulations that account for path-dependent market reactions across multiple timescales. Expected outcomes include a novel risk propagation metric quantifying contagion susceptibility in hybrid financial ecosystems, scenario analysis tools for monitoring emergent vulnerabilities in derivative collateral chains, and sensitivity benchmarks comparing centralized versus decentralized risk mitigation strategies. By leveraging GPU-accelerated tensor operations and distributed memory architectures, this work aims to advance predictive capabilities for systemic crisis prevention while establishing computational best practices for next-generation financial network analysis. The resulting tools will provide institutions and regulators with actionable insights into cross-market risk amplification mechanisms that conventional value-at-risk models currently overlook.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the strategies used to define and manage acceptable financial risk for companies. Includes instruction in banking and bank regulations, derivative securities, interest rate and credit markets, financial engineering of systematic risk, and equity, bond, futures, and options markets.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of narrative structures and stylistic features across British and Commonwealth literary works from the 18th century to the present. Traditional literary scholarship, constrained by manual close-reading methods, struggles to systematically examine large-scale textual patterns spanning centuries and diverse geographies. This research addresses this gap by employing computational text analysis and machine learning techniques to interrogate a corpus of over 50,000 novels, plays, and poetic works digitized through partnerships with the British Library and the Commonwealth Archives. Using natural language processing (NLP) pipelines optimized for historical texts, the project will quantify syntactic complexity, lexical diversity, and thematic shifts across periods and regions. Stylometric algorithms will identify authorial fingerprints and trace intertextual influences, while graph-based network models will map the diffusion of narrative tropes across Commonwealth literatures. HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based models on archaic linguistic forms and parallelizing computationally intensive tasks such as topic modeling at scale. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated texts, visualizations of literary trends, and scholarly articles re-evaluating canon formation in postcolonial contexts. By bridging computational methods with literary theory, this project aims to uncover macro-level patterns in the development of Anglophone literatures, offering new insights into the cultural dynamics of the British Empire and its legacy in contemporary writing.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the literatures and literary developments of the English-speaking peoples of the British Isles and the British Commonwealth, from the origins of the English language to the present. Includes instruction in period and genre studies, author studies, country and regional specializations, literary criticism, and the study of folkloric traditions.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamic interplay between personality traits, neurophysiological markers, and contextual behavioral responses through computational modeling, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to overcome existing methodological limitations. Traditional personality psychology frameworks—such as Freudian, Skinnerian, and Rogerian models—often rely on static, reductionist assessments, limiting their ability to capture the temporal and multi-layered complexity of personality as a system. To address this, we propose developing an integrative agent-based model (ABM) that simulates how stable personality characteristics interact with situational variables and neurophysiological processes (e.g., stress-response pathways, dopaminergic activation) to shape behavior. The ABM will incorporate parameters derived from empirical datasets, including longitudinal behavioral studies, functional neuroimaging, and psychopharmacological interventions, to test competing hypotheses about trait-state interactions. Machine learning algorithms will be applied to optimize model fit and identify nonlinear patterns in high-dimensional data. HPC resources are critical for scaling simulations across diverse theoretical scenarios (e.g., trait activation thresholds, reinforcement learning dynamics) and conducting Bayesian parameter estimation with large posterior distributions. Expected outcomes include a validated computational framework that reconciles divergent theories of personality structure and generates testable predictions about individual differences in adaptive and maladaptive behaviors. This work will provide novel insights into the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying personality, bridging gaps between psychodynamic, behavioral, and physiological perspectives. The resulting open-source tools and simulated datasets will serve as a resource for the broader research community, enabling hypothesis-driven exploration of personality dynamics at unprecedented granularity. By integrating historically siloed theories within a unified computational architecture, this project aims to advance personality psychology into a new era of data-intensive, theory-generative science.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the unique organization of fairly permanent characteristics that set the individual apart from other individuals and, at the same time, determine how others respond to that individual. Includes instruction in Freudian, Skinnerian, Rogerian, and Ellisonian psychology; neo-Freudian psychology; psychological systems, neurophysiology, and psychopharmacology.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of misinformation diffusion across digital media platforms through advanced computational modeling, addressing critical gaps in understanding how cultural, social, and technological variables influence communication patterns. While prior research has explored misinformation spread in homogeneous groups, few studies account for the interplay of intercultural communication norms, algorithmic amplification, and multimodal content (e.g., text, images, video) in shaping large-scale dissemination. Our work integrates communication theory with computational social science methods to analyze multi-platform datasets (Twitter, TikTok, and Reddit) encompassing 50 million posts, with metadata on user demographics, network structures, and engagement metrics. Using high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will implement a three-phase approach: (1) automated content analysis via transformer-based NLP models fine-tuned for cross-cultural linguistic nuances and multimodal disinformation detection; (2) temporal network analysis using dynamic graph neural networks to map community-specific diffusion pathways; and (3) agent-based simulations modeling intercultural communication behaviors under varying platform moderation scenarios. Computational demands include processing terabyte-scale datasets, training multimodal deep learning architectures, and running parallelized simulations across 10,000+ parameter combinations. Expected outcomes include a framework for predicting misinformation propagation across cultural boundaries, validated through case studies on climate change and public health narratives. Results will advance communication theories of intercultural influence while providing actionable insights for platform designers and policymakers. The project’s scale necessitates HPC capabilities for distributed storage, GPU-accelerated model training, and large-memory simulations beyond typical departmental computing infrastructure. By bridging communication studies with computational methodologies, this work aims to establish novel paradigms for studying digital discourse at unprecedented granularity and cultural specificity.
cip_definition: An program that focuses on the comprehensive study of communication, research and research methods, and theories of communication, and that spans specialties within the field of communications. Includes instruction in interpersonal, group, organizational, and intercultural communication; quantitative and qualitative methods of inquiry; critical thinking, argumentation, and persuasion; media, society, and culture; consequences and effects of mass media; and media social science and criticism.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in Tribal/Indigenous Law, specifically addressing the challenge of analyzing complex, large-scale legal and cultural datasets critical to understanding the interplay between tribal sovereignty, historical treaties, and contemporary legal frameworks. Tribal legal systems and Indigenous rights discourse generate multifaceted data, including digitized historical records, oral histories, treaty texts, court decisions, and ethnographic materials, which are often fragmented across repositories or embedded in non-standardized formats. Traditional legal research methods struggle to synthesize these datasets at scale, limiting insights into systemic patterns of rights violations, policy impacts, or cultural preservation needs. The proposed research will employ computational text analysis, network modeling, and machine learning techniques to (1) identify correlations between historical treaty language and modern judicial interpretations, (2) map the evolution of tribal governance structures in response to federal policies, and (3) simulate the potential impacts of proposed legislation on Indigenous resource rights. Custom NLP pipelines will process multilingual and non-textual sources (e.g., oral tradition transcripts), while graph-based algorithms will model relationships between legal entities across temporal and jurisdictional boundaries. HPC resources are essential to handle the volume and heterogeneity of data, enable parallel processing of linguistically diverse materials, and support iterative scenario testing. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible computational toolkit for tribal legal practitioners, policy simulations to inform advocacy strategies, and novel methodologies for centering Indigenous epistemologies in sociolegal data analysis. This work bridges computational social science and critical legal studies, offering a model for ethically engaged, community-responsive research that amplifies Indigenous self-determination in legal discourse.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law, policies, and regulations affecting federal Indian law, tribal law and policy, and Indigenous peoples' human rights.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a novel computational framework for enhancing the detection and analysis of systemic risk patterns in real-time auditing processes. Traditional auditing methodologies often struggle to integrate dynamic, high-volume transactional data with contextual operational variables, leading to delayed risk identification and reactive compliance measures. The proposed work addresses this gap by constructing a multi-agent simulation environment that models complex interactions between financial transactions, regulatory constraints, and organizational behavior across decentralized supply chains. The computational approach combines graph-based anomaly detection algorithms with reinforcement learning to identify latent risk pathways and simulate audit scenarios under varying regulatory conditions. Key challenges include processing heterogeneous datasets (e.g., blockchain-ledger transactions, IoT-enabled operational logs, and unstructured compliance documents) and maintaining temporal consistency in risk assessments at enterprise scale. HPC resources will enable parallelized execution of Monte Carlo simulations to quantify uncertainty in audit outcomes while training deep learning models on historical audit findings across multiple industries. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for predictive audit analytics, capable of generating probabilistic risk heatmaps and optimizing resource allocation for audit teams. The research will specifically examine applications in cross-jurisdictional cryptocurrency transactions and AI-driven financial reporting systems, areas where current auditing standards lack computational rigor. By enabling real-time, data-driven audit prioritization, this work aims to reduce compliance costs by an estimated 15–20% in pilot sectors while establishing a foundation for adaptive regulatory frameworks in emerging digital economies. The computational infrastructure developed will be scalable to public auditing entities and private firms managing multi-tiered compliance requirements.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, including certified accountants, to perform independent internal and external appraisals to evaluate organizational financial and operational activities, ensure compliance with laws and policies, safeguard assets, and promote effective planning and resource allocation. Includes instruction in advanced accounting, audit tools and techniques, sampling, risk and control, audit planning, audit function management, law and regulations, environmental auditing, information technology applications, professional standards and ethics, and specific industry and service sector problems.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance anthropological research on the dynamics of cultural transmission and adaptation in prehistoric human populations. A central challenge in anthropological modeling is simulating large-scale, multi-generational behavioral interactions under variable ecological and social constraints, which requires computationally intensive agent-based models (ABMs) and probabilistic analyses of sparse archaeological datasets. Current limitations in local computing infrastructure prevent the exploration of parameter spaces necessary to address key questions: How did resource volatility and social network structures interact to shape cultural resilience in early Holocene societies? What computational frameworks can best integrate heterogeneous data (e.g., artifact distributions, paleoenvironmental proxies, and ethnographic analogs) to infer decision-making processes in past populations? To address these gaps, we propose deploying scalable ABMs on HPC clusters to simulate population interactions across millennia, incorporating dynamically linked environmental, demographic, and cultural variables. Parallelized Bayesian inference methods will be applied to archaeological datasets spanning 10,000–5,000 BP from six continental regions, enabling comparative analysis of technological innovation rates under differing climate regimes. The computational workflow will utilize containerized environments for reproducibility, with iterative model calibration against radiocarbon-dated cultural sequences. Expected outcomes include: (1) quantitative estimates of threshold conditions for cultural fragmentation versus continuity in early agricultural societies, (2) open-source tools for simulating anthropogenic landscape modifications, and (3) a publicly accessible database linking archaeological signatures to simulated social processes. By enabling complex systems approaches at previously impractical scales, this work will establish new methodologies for testing anthropological theories of cultural evolution while providing frameworks to analyze modern societal resilience through long-term human-environment dynamics. The requested resources are critical for managing memory-intensive phylogenetic analyses of cultural trait diffusion and Monte Carlo simulations assessing demographic uncertainty in prehistoric contexts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of human beings, their antecedents and related primates, and their cultural behavior and institutions, in comparative perspective. Includes instruction in biological/physical anthropology, primatology, human paleontology and prehistoric archeology, hominid evolution, anthropological linguistics, ethnography, ethnology, ethnohistory, socio-cultural anthropology, psychological anthropology, research methods, and applications to areas such as medicine, forensic pathology, museum studies, and international affairs.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to quantify and mitigate systemic risks in insurance markets, particularly those arising from interconnected economic, environmental, and demographic factors. Traditional actuarial methods often rely on simplified assumptions that inadequately capture the nonlinear dependencies and tail risks inherent in large-scale systems, such as climate-related catastrophes or pandemic-driven health and economic crises. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework integrating stochastic simulation, agent-based modeling, and machine learning to analyze multi-domain risk interactions. The research will parameterize models using heterogeneous datasets—including insurance claims, climate projections, demographic trends, and real-time economic indicators—to simulate cascading risk scenarios under varying regulatory and environmental conditions. Key computational challenges include scaling Monte Carlo methods for high-dimensional uncertainty propagation, optimizing gradient-based solvers for dynamic risk allocation, and training neural networks to identify latent risk correlations across disparate data streams. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallelized execution of millions of scenario iterations, sensitivity analyses, and real-time calibration against emerging data. Expected outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible library of modular risk simulation tools tailored for actuarial applications, (2) empirically validated metrics for capital adequacy under compound stress scenarios, and (3) policy insights for managing systemic risks in sectors such as catastrophe reinsurance and longevity-based financial products. By leveraging distributed computing architectures, this work will overcome memory and latency constraints that limit conventional actuarial software, providing insurers and regulators with scalable tools to address 21st-century risk landscapes. The resource request supports GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning tasks and high-memory nodes for large-scale optimization, ensuring robust handling of datasets exceeding 100TB in size.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the mathematical and statistical analysis of risk, and their applications to insurance and other business management problems. Includes instruction in forecasting theory, quantitative and non-quantitative risk measurement methodologies, development of risk tables, secondary data analysis, and computer-assisted research methods.

abstract: Women’s health research faces unique challenges due to the biological, social, and environmental complexity underlying sex-specific conditions. This project addresses critical gaps in understanding the molecular mechanisms of understudied women’s health conditions, including endometriosis, preeclampsia, and hormone-responsive cancers, through integrative computational modeling. A key barrier to progress is the limited ability to analyze high-dimensional datasets—spanning genomics, proteomics, electronic health records, and imaging—while accounting for dynamic hormonal interactions and population-level heterogeneity. To overcome this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework combining machine learning, multiscale simulations, and genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The computational workflow will integrate multi-omics data from clinical cohorts (n > 50,000) to identify subtype-specific biomarkers and predictive signatures for disease risk, progression, and therapeutic response. Deep learning models will map hormone receptor interactions across tissues, while agent-based simulations will model cellular microenvironment dynamics in conditions like uterine fibroid growth. Large-scale parallelization will enable iterative optimization of these models across parameter spaces and validation against independent clinical datasets. Anticipated outcomes include the discovery of novel therapeutic targets for endometriosis, risk stratification tools for preeclampsia, and mechanistic insights into racial disparities in gynecologic cancer outcomes. By leveraging HPC resources, this project will overcome current limitations in data processing speed, model complexity, and reproducibility, enabling transformative insights into conditions that disproportionately affect women. Results will be disseminated through open-source tools for gender-aware health analytics, fostering collaboration in women’s health research. This work directly aligns with national priorities to reduce health inequities and advance precision medicine for underrepresented populations in clinical research.
cip_definition: Research focused on Women's Health

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the molecular and systems-level mechanisms underlying synergistic botanical formulations used in naturopathic medicine. While naturopathy emphasizes multi-modal, natural therapies to promote self-healing, the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic interactions of complex plant-derived compounds remain poorly characterized, limiting evidence-based optimization of clinical protocols. The research addresses this gap by analyzing how polyherbal formulations modulate immune-neuro-endocrine networks, with a focus on low-dose botanical combinations that exhibit non-linear bioactivity—a phenomenon observed clinically but inadequately explained by reductionist models. Computational workflows will integrate molecular docking simulations, machine learning-driven network pharmacology, and multi-omics data fusion to map interactions between phytochemical ensembles and human proteomic targets. A novel computational framework will be developed to model entourage effects—the emergent therapeutic properties arising from compound interactions—using quantum chemistry-informed molecular dynamics simulations to assess energy landscapes of botanical mixtures. Concurrently, Bayesian network models will correlate in silico predictions with existing clinical metabolomic datasets from patients undergoing naturopathic treatments for chronic inflammatory conditions. The HPC environment is critical for scaling these analyses across thousands of potential phytochemical combinations and simulating temporal biological responses at cellular resolution. Expected outcomes include the identification of key synergistic phytochemical pairs, predictive biomarkers for treatment personalization, and a publicly accessible database linking traditional naturopathic pharmacopeia to molecular interaction profiles. By elucidating mechanisms underlying holistic therapeutic strategies, this work aims to establish a computational foundation for advancing naturopathic research methodologies while fostering interdisciplinary dialogue between traditional medicine systems and computational biology. The resource request directly supports the development of open-source tools for natural product research, addressing a critical need in integrative health sciences for scalable approaches to study complex, multi-target interventions.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of naturopathic medicine, an holistic therapeutic approach combining medical knowledge with noninvasive natural, homeopathic, and non-Western therapies and emphasizing disease prevention, wellness, and self-healing. Includes instruction in the basic medical sciences, epidemiology, neuroscience, biostatistics, public and community health, laboratory and clinical diagnosis, pharmacognosy, botanical medicine, homeopathy, principles of Oriental medicine and Ayurveda, manipulative therapy, naturopathic therapeutics, therapeutic nutrition, case analysis and management, philosophy of naturopathy, patient counseling, practice management, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the study of personality structure and dynamics by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model the interplay between stable personality traits, situational variability, and neurophysiological mechanisms. Traditional personality psychology relies on cross-sectional or longitudinal self-report data, which often struggle to disentangle enduring traits from transient states or contextual influences. To address this, we propose a computational framework integrating dynamic systems modeling, machine learning, and multilevel Bayesian analyses to simulate and predict how individual differences in traits such as neuroticism, extraversion, and conscientiousness interact with real-time environmental cues and neural activation patterns. The project will analyze existing large-scale datasets (e.g., multimodal behavioral assessments, fMRI studies, and experience-sampling metadata) and generate synthetic data via agent-based models to test competing theories of personality coherence across contexts. Key computational challenges include scaling hierarchical models to accommodate high-dimensional data (e.g., trait-state interactions across 10,000+ simulated agents), optimizing reinforcement learning algorithms to map decision-making patterns onto trait profiles, and conducting parallelized neurophysiological network analyses. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated open-source toolkit for simulating personality-environment interactions, (2) evidence-based revisions to trait-situation debate frameworks, and (3) novel hypotheses linking dopaminergic/serotonergic system dynamics to trait stability. By quantifying how neurophysiological constraints mediate trait expression, this work aims to unify disparate theoretical traditions (e.g., Freudian drive models and Skinnerian behavioral approaches) within a computationally testable paradigm. The requested HPC resources are critical for managing memory-intensive simulations, reducing runtime for iterative model comparisons, and enabling large-scale parameter space explorations that are infeasible on standard lab infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the unique organization of fairly permanent characteristics that set the individual apart from other individuals and, at the same time, determine how others respond to that individual. Includes instruction in Freudian, Skinnerian, Rogerian, and Ellisonian psychology; neo-Freudian psychology; psychological systems, neurophysiology, and psychopharmacology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model and analyze the efficacy of adaptive teaching strategies in diverse K-12 classroom environments. A critical challenge in teacher education is understanding how dynamic factors—such as student engagement, differentiated instruction, and socio-cultural dynamics—interact in real time to shape learning outcomes. Traditional qualitative and small-scale quantitative studies struggle to capture the complexity of these interactions, particularly when scaling insights across varied demographic contexts. To address this, we propose developing a computational framework using agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning (ML) to simulate classroom ecosystems. The ABM component will integrate empirical data on student behaviors, instructor decision-making patterns, and environmental variables (e.g., technology access, peer interactions) to create virtual classrooms reflecting urban, suburban, and rural settings. Concurrently, ML algorithms will process longitudinal datasets from national education surveys and localized classroom observations to identify patterns in instructional effectiveness. HPC resources are essential to handle the high-dimensional parameter space of these models, including real-time adjustments for variables such as equity-focused interventions, trauma-informed practices, and the integration of generative AI tools in lesson planning. Expected outcomes include a scalable predictive tool to help educators optimize teaching strategies for heterogeneous student groups, as well as evidence-based insights into how systemic inequities manifest in classroom dynamics. This work aligns with the program’s emphasis on school reform and the intersection of technology, theory, and practice in teacher preparation. By simulating scenarios that are logistically or ethically challenging to replicate in live settings, the project aims to advance data-driven teacher training paradigms while preserving the human-centered focus of education.
detailed_field: Teacher education, specific levels and methods
cip_definition: Any instructional program in teacher education that prepares individuals to be effective educators or trainers. Includes instruction in school reform and design; arts and technology in the classroom; theories of teaching and learning; adult and adolescent development; race, class, and gender dynamics; and the history and future of education in America.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to enhance the integration and predictive analysis of multi-domain intelligence data for military decision-making. Modern intelligence operations require synthesizing vast, heterogeneous datasets—including signals intelligence (SIGINT), human intelligence (HUMINT), geospatial data, and open-source information—to identify emerging threats and optimize resource deployment. However, traditional analytical tools struggle with the scale, velocity, and unstructured nature of these data streams, particularly in dynamic operational environments. This research addresses the critical gap in scalable, real-time processing and pattern recognition across classified and unclassified sources, enabling proactive threat anticipation. The project will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement distributed machine learning models, graph-based network analysis, and natural language processing (NLP) pipelines tailored to military intelligence workflows. Key computational challenges include federated learning across secure data silos, anomaly detection in temporally evolving networks, and semantic extraction from multilingual, noisy text. By parallelizing these tasks across GPU clusters and optimizing memory-intensive graph traversals, the framework aims to reduce latency in situational awareness products from hours to minutes. Expected outcomes include an open architecture toolkit for adaptive intelligence fusion, validated against historical operational datasets, and novel algorithms for identifying latent adversarial tactics. Success will provide military planners with a unified platform to simulate threat scenarios, assess resource allocation trade-offs, and prioritize collection assets. This work bridges computational scalability with domain-specific operational constraints, advancing the intelligence community’s capacity to preempt asymmetric threats while maintaining rigorous security and chain-of-command protocols. The requested HPC resources will enable benchmarking at operationally relevant data scales, ensuring translational impact for joint all-domain command and control (JADC2) initiatives.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and techniques of intelligence acquisition, analysis and exploitation. Includes instruction in intelligence organizations, the intelligence cycle, intelligence operations planning, intelligence analysis and reporting, intelligence methods, electronic and signals intelligence, operations and communications security, human intelligence management, intelligence chain of command, information exploitation and psychological warfare, and the relationship to national security policy and strategy.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the structural and cultural evolution of European urban centers between 1500 and 1800, a period marked by rapid demographic growth, economic transformation, and shifting political frameworks. The research problem centers on identifying patterns of urbanization and their correlation with socioeconomic factors—such as trade networks, institutional development, and technological innovation—across diverse regions, including the Mediterranean, Western Europe, and the Baltic. Traditional historiographical methods struggle to synthesize the vast, fragmented datasets required for such comparative analysis, including digitized municipal records, tax registers, migration logs, and cartographic materials. To address this, the project will employ computational text analysis, geospatial modeling, and network analysis tools to process multilingual archival sources, map demographic shifts, and reconstruct economic interactions at scale. Machine learning classifiers will be trained to categorize qualitative data from civic chronicles and guild records, enabling systematic analysis of cultural narratives alongside quantitative trends. The HPC environment is critical for handling the volume and complexity of these datasets, which include over 10 million structured and unstructured records from 30 repositories, as well as high-resolution georeferenced maps. Expected outcomes include (1) a dynamic, open-access database of urban indicators, (2) visualizations of regional interconnectedness and resource flows, and (3) statistical models testing hypotheses about the role of institutions in mitigating crises like famine or plague. By integrating computational methods with archival research, this project aims to advance transnational perspectives on early modern European history, offering new insights into how cities shaped—and were shaped by—broader societal transformations. The findings will contribute to scholarly debates on state formation, economic resilience, and the longue durée impacts of urbanization, while demonstrating the value of HPC-driven methodologies in historical research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the development of European society, culture, and institutions from the origins to the present. Includes instruction in European historiography, European history sources and materials, historical research methods, and applications to the study of specific themes, issues, periods, and institutions.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the pedagogical efficacy and cultural adaptability of digital religious education curricula across diverse global faith communities. While religious education programs are critical for sustaining traditions, existing studies rarely address how digitally mediated instruction—such as virtual scripture study, AI-driven moral reasoning simulations, or cross-cultural interfaith dialogue platforms—impacts learning outcomes in varied socioreligious contexts. The computational challenge lies in modeling complex, nonlinear relationships between instructional design variables (e.g., multimedia integration, adaptive feedback systems) and learner engagement metrics across disparate datasets, which include multilingual textual corpora, behavioral interaction logs, and ethnographic surveys from over 20 religious traditions. Using a mixed-methods framework, the project will apply natural language processing (NLP) to classify thematic patterns in learner feedback, agent-based modeling to simulate community-specific adoption of digital tools, and deep learning architectures to predict long-term knowledge retention rates. HPC resources are essential for processing terabytes of unstructured data, training multimodal neural networks, and running large-scale sensitivity analyses on pedagogical parameters. Anticipated outcomes include a scalable computational model for optimizing faith-specific educational interventions, an open-access repository of annotated intercultural religious education datasets, and evidence-based guidelines for mitigating biases in AI-generated spiritual content. By bridging computational social science and religious pedagogy, this work aims to establish a methodological foundation for data-driven decision-making in religious education—a field historically reliant on qualitative approaches—while addressing urgent gaps in equitable resource allocation for underrepresented faith communities in digital spaces.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory and practice of providing educational services to members of faith communities, within the context of a particular religion, and that prepares individuals to serve as religious educators. Includes instruction in planning and teaching lessons, organizing and supervising instructional activities, designing and developing instructional materials, and administering religious education programs and facilities.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize instructional strategies for postsecondary STEM courses by modeling the relationship between teaching methods, learner engagement, and educational outcomes through large-scale computational analysis. Despite advances in learning science, many instructors lack evidence-based frameworks to dynamically adapt course designs across diverse classroom contexts. The research problem centers on identifying computationally detectable patterns in multimodal educational datasets—including LMS interaction logs, formative assessment performance, and classroom observation metrics—to guide real-time pedagogical adjustments. We propose developing machine learning models trained on anonymized datasets from 150+ university courses (spanning physics, biology, and engineering disciplines) to cluster effective teaching practices under varying enrollment sizes, student preparedness levels, and modality constraints (in-person/hybrid/online). The computational approach combines natural language processing of syllabus artifacts, temporal graph analysis of discussion forum interactions, and agent-based simulations of motivation dynamics. High-performance computing resources are essential for processing >50TB of heterogeneous data, running parallelized hyperparameter optimization for deep neural networks predicting student success, and conducting Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses on instructional design variables. Expected outcomes include (1) an open-source toolkit for quantifying alignment between course structures and evidence-based andragogical principles, (2) predictive models to help instructors prioritize syllabus modifications, and (3) generative AI prototypes that recommend personalized teaching strategies based on institutional context and learner analytics. By establishing computational links between micro-level classroom decisions and macro-level educational outcomes, this work aims to advance discipline-specific teacher development while maintaining rigorous ethical standards for educational data stewardship. The resource-intensive simulations and large-language model fine-tuning required for this research necessitate GPU-accelerated computing clusters capable of sustained throughput for complex ensemble modeling tasks.
detailed_field: Teacher education, specific levels and methods
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach at a postsecondary institution. Includes instruction in andragogy, assessment, classroom motivation, instructional design and technology, learner-centered teaching, learning science, syllabus construction, and teaching critical thinking.

abstract: In the domain of film and photographic preservation, the degradation of archival materials poses a significant challenge to cultural heritage conservation. Traditional restoration techniques, while effective, are labor-intensive and struggle to scale with the vast quantities of high-resolution media held in archives. This project seeks to address this bottleneck by developing computational workflows that leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to automate and enhance the restoration of degraded film and photographic collections. The research focuses on training deep neural networks—including generative adversarial networks (GANs) and vision transformers—to perform tasks such as noise reduction, scratch removal, and color stabilization across large datasets of 4K-resolution scans. These models require processing terabytes of image sequences with frame-specific temporal coherence, necessitating parallelized GPU-accelerated workflows and distributed storage systems accessible only through HPC infrastructure. Additionally, the project will explore the use of physics-based simulations to model historical film degradation processes, enabling synthetic data generation to improve model generalizability. The outcomes aim to produce open-source tools for archivists, significantly reducing the time and cost associated with large-scale preservation efforts while advancing computational methodologies in media conservation. By integrating artistic sensibilities with machine learning pipelines, this work bridges technical innovation with the ethical and aesthetic considerations inherent in visual heritage stewardship, offering a template for interdisciplinary collaboration in digital humanities and computational arts.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
cip_title: Film/ Video and Photographic Arts, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in film/video and photographic arts, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The increasing volume of digitized and born-digital archival materials presents significant challenges in metadata generation, sensitivity assessment, and long-term preservation. Traditional archival workflows, reliant on manual appraisal and description, struggle to scale with heterogeneous, large-scale collections, risking information inaccessibility or inadvertent exposure of private data. This project seeks to address these challenges through the development of computational tools that leverage machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) to automate metadata extraction, classify sensitive content, and model preservation risks in archival datasets. The research will utilize high-performance computing (HPC) resources to train and deploy deep learning models on corpus-scale datasets, including digitized text, images, and complex digital objects (e.g., emails, spreadsheets). Key computational tasks include fine-tuning transformer-based architectures for context-aware metadata tagging, optimizing computer vision pipelines for handwritten document analysis, and simulating decay patterns in digital file formats under varying preservation conditions. By parallelizing workflows across GPU nodes, the project aims to process multi-terabyte collections efficiently, enabling rapid identification of personally identifiable information (PII) for redaction and generating probabilistic models to prioritize archival interventions for at-risk formats. Anticipated outcomes include open-source software tools for archivists, validated frameworks for integrating computational methods into existing archival standards, and a public benchmark dataset for evaluating archival ML applications. This work bridges archival science, data ethics, and computational linguistics, offering scalable solutions to enhance accessibility while addressing ethical and legal responsibilities in digital stewardship. The requested HPC resources are critical to handling the computational complexity of multimodal data analysis and ensuring reproducible, institution-agnostic methodologies for the archival community.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to identify, manage, preserve, and make available records with long-term value for documentation, legal, research, and other purposes. Includes instruction in appraisal and collection development, information and records management, archival preservation, access systems, management of electronic records, archival outreach, and legal and ethical issues.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in public transportation resource allocation by developing a dynamic optimization framework to balance demand, equity, and sustainability in multimodal transit systems. Urbanization and shifting mobility patterns have strained existing infrastructure, leading to service gaps, congestion, and inequitable access. Traditional allocation models often rely on static datasets and fail to account for real-time behavioral feedback, environmental impacts, or equity trade-offs. To overcome these limitations, we propose a computational approach integrating agent-based modeling, machine learning, and high-dimensional optimization. Using anonymized smart card data, traffic sensor feeds, and socioeconomic datasets, we will simulate commuter behavior across transportation modes under varying policy scenarios. Reinforcement learning algorithms will iteratively optimize resource distribution—such as fleet deployment, route adjustments, and pricing incentives—while constrained by equity metrics and emissions targets. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to manage the complexity of simulating millions of individual agents, processing real-time data streams, and solving combinatorial optimization problems at metropolitan scales. Expected outcomes include a decision-support tool for transit agencies to dynamically allocate resources in response to demand shocks, such as extreme weather or public health crises, while minimizing service disparities. The project will also quantify trade-offs between operational efficiency, carbon reduction, and accessibility for low-income populations. By aligning computational modeling with public administration priorities, this work aims to advance data-driven strategies for equitable and sustainable mobility management. Results will be disseminated through open-source code repositories, partnerships with regional transit authorities, and policy briefs targeting transportation economists and urban planners.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory, policy, law, and practices required to administrate and operate public transportation facilities, networks, services, and systems. Includes instruction in demand analysis and forecasting, environmental planning, facilities design and construction, geographic information systems (GIS), logistics, multi- and intermodal transportation systems, project management, public administration, public policy, transportation economics, transportation law, transportation operations, transportation systems, and transportation technologies.

abstract: The proposed research aims to elucidate the dynamic behavior of membrane-embedded ion channels and transporters, focusing on their conformational transitions under physiologically relevant mechanical and electrochemical gradients. These proteins are critical for cellular signaling and homeostasis, yet their structural rearrangements during gating or solute transport remain poorly resolved due to limitations in experimental temporal resolution and the complexity of lipid-protein interactions. This project addresses these gaps through large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to model full-length protein systems in realistic lipid bilayers, capturing microseconds-to-millisecond timescale dynamics. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will employ all-atom and coarse-grained MD simulations using AMBER and GROMACS, integrating adaptive sampling techniques and machine learning-accelerated free energy calculations to map rare conformational states. Systems of interest include the Piezo1 mechanosensitive channel and the sodium-glucose transporter SGLT1, both embedded in asymmetric membranes with varying lipid compositions. The computational workflow will combine enhanced sampling (metadynamics, replica exchange) with continuum solvent-electrostatics modeling to quantify the interplay between membrane curvature, tension, and voltage-dependent activation. Expected outcomes include (1) atomistic models of force transduction pathways in Piezo1, explaining how mechanical stimuli propagate from the lipid bilayer to the channel gate, and (2) energetics profiles of SGLT1’s alternating-access mechanism under physiological sodium gradients. These results will advance fundamental understanding of biophysical principles governing membrane protein function while providing testable hypotheses for collaborative electrophysiology and cryo-EM studies. The requested HPC allocation (∼500,000 CPU-hr, GPU-accelerated nodes) is essential to achieve sufficient sampling given the >1 million atom system sizes and the need for multiple replicates under varying thermodynamic conditions. This work bridges molecular-scale dynamics with cellular-level physiology, offering insights critical for designing targeted therapies in channelopathies and metabolic disorders.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of physics principles to the scientific study of the mechanisms of biological processes and assemblies at all levels of complexity. Includes instruction in research methods and equipment operation and applications to subjects such as bioenergetics, biophysical theory and modeling, electrophysics, membrane biology, channels, receptors and transporters, contractility and muscle function, protein shaping and folding, molecular and supramolecular structures and assemblies, and computational science.

abstract: Geothermal energy systems represent a critical component of renewable energy infrastructure, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by challenges in optimizing installation configurations, predicting long-term performance, and mitigating equipment degradation under variable subsurface conditions. This project seeks to address these challenges through high-fidelity computational modeling of geothermal heat exchange systems, focusing on the interplay between equipment design, geological heterogeneity, and operational parameters. The research will employ multiphysics simulations to model coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical processes in geothermal boreholes, heat pumps, and distribution networks. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve transient 3D simulations of heat transfer in anisotropic geological formations, stress analysis of mechanical components under thermal cycling, and machine learning-driven optimization of system layouts. Computational workflows will integrate finite element analysis (FEA) for structural integrity assessment, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for working fluid behavior, and Monte Carlo methods to quantify uncertainty in subsurface property estimates. The project will validate models against field data from existing installations provided by industry partners. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for equipment lifespan estimation, optimized borehole spacing configurations tailored to regional geology, and decision-support frameworks for proactive maintenance scheduling. These results will directly inform curriculum updates in geothermal technician training programs, bridging the gap between field practices and computational analytics. By enabling precise virtual prototyping of geothermal systems, this work aims to reduce installation costs by 15-20% and extend functional system lifetimes, advancing the technical workforce's capacity to deploy robust geothermal solutions in diverse geological settings.
cip_title: Geothermal Energy System Installation and Repair Technology/ Technician
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to assemble, install, operate, maintain, and repair geothermal energy systems. Includes instruction in installing, maintaining and testing various types of equipment.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational tools to model and analyze speech production and language processing impairments in individuals with communication disorders, with a focus on improving diagnostic precision and therapeutic outcomes. Current clinical assessments for disorders such as aphasia, dysarthria, and pediatric speech-sound disorders rely on manual, time-intensive analyses of speech samples, which lack the granularity to capture subtle kinematic, acoustic, and linguistic features predictive of pathology progression or treatment responsiveness. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating high-resolution biomechanical simulations of vocal tract dynamics, deep learning-based acoustic pattern recognition, and natural language processing (NLP) models to quantify disordered speech and language patterns. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to train neural networks on multimodal datasets (including audio, articulatory kinematics, and fMRI-derived neuroimaging data), simulate fluid-structure interactions during swallowing and phonation, and optimize real-time analysis pipelines for clinical deployment. The project will leverage GPU-accelerated frameworks like PyTorch and FEniCS to parallelize finite element modeling of vocal fold vibrations and transformer-based NLP architectures for parsing syntactically complex language samples. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models linking specific articulatory biomechanics deficits to perceptual speech intelligibility metrics, (2) automated tools for detecting subclinical language deterioration in neurodegenerative populations, and (3) open-source software enabling clinicians to personalize therapy targets using patient-specific computational profiles. By bridging computational linguistics and motor speech physiology, this work aims to establish scalable, data-driven paradigms for speech-language pathology that enhance both research and clinical practice.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to evaluate the speaking, language interpretation, and related physiological and cognitive capabilities of children and/or adults and develop treatment and rehabilitative solutions in consultation with clinicians and educators. Includes instruction in the anatomy and physiology of speech and hearing, biomechanics of swallowing and vocal articulation, communications disorders, psychology of auditory function and cognitive communication, language assessment and diagnostic techniques, and rehabilitative and management therapies.

abstract: Agricultural production systems face increasing pressure to optimize resource efficiency and resilience amid climate variability and evolving pest-disease pressures. This project seeks to develop a computational framework for simulating multi-scale interactions between crop genotypes, management practices, and environmental stressors to identify sustainable intensification strategies. We propose integrating high-resolution soil sensor data, climate projections, and genomic information into a coupled modeling system that combines process-based crop growth models with machine learning architectures. The core computational challenge involves parameterizing genotype-environment-management (G×E×M) relationships across spatial scales from individual plants to production fields, requiring iterative simulations of >10^6 possible scenario combinations. High-performance computing resources are essential for three components: 1) Parallelized execution of modified DSSAT-CROPGRO modules with custom stress response algorithms, 2) Training convolutional neural networks on hyperspectral imagery and LiDAR data to detect subfield nutrient deficiencies, and 3) Bayesian optimization of irrigation/nutrient application schedules using 10-year regional climate model ensembles. Initial pilot studies on soybean systems have demonstrated model feasibility but were constrained by 48-hour simulation bottlenecks when evaluating 50,000+ parameter sets. The requested allocation would enable daily canopy-scale resolution across 500ha virtual fields through GPU-accelerated cellular automata models, representing a 40× scalability improvement. Expected outcomes include open-source decision support tools for precision nitrogen management and genomic selection indices for drought-adaptive root architecture traits. By quantifying tradeoffs between yield stability and input costs under climate uncertainty, this work directly addresses priority gaps in digital agriculture infrastructure while adhering to FAIR data principles. The computational pipelines developed will provide transferable frameworks for optimizing diverse cropping systems, with particular relevance to row crop operations in water-limited environments.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences

abstract: Current educational systems face challenges in ensuring equitable access to linguistically appropriate learning materials, particularly in multilingual and underserved regions. This project seeks to address the gap in understanding how linguistic complexity within curricular texts influences student comprehension and educational outcomes. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques to analyze a corpus of over 10 million pages of educational materials across 50 languages, assessing syntactic structures, lexical diversity, and readability metrics. Concurrently, we will integrate longitudinal student performance data from international assessments to model relationships between text complexity and learning efficacy. Computational challenges include parallel processing of large-scale text datasets, training multilingual transformer models for complexity classification, and running mixed-effects regression analyses to account for socio-contextual variables. The expected outcomes include a scalable framework for evaluating linguistic accessibility, evidence-based guidelines for curriculum design, and policy recommendations to mitigate disparities in material availability. By bridging computational linguistics and educational equity, this research aims to provide actionable insights for global educational stakeholders, fostering inclusive pedagogical practices and informing resource allocation strategies in diverse linguistic landscapes.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general theory, practice, organization of, and public policies in education. Includes instruction in learning and teaching, the basic principles of educational psychology, the art of teaching, the planning and administration of educational activities, school safety and health issues, and the social foundations of education.

abstract: The increasing complexity of genomic and phenotypic datasets in livestock research necessitates advanced computational tools to address challenges in precision breeding and disease resilience. This project seeks to develop a scalable framework for integrating multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics) to identify genetic markers associated with disease resistance in swine populations. Current methods struggle to process high-dimensional datasets efficiently, limiting the discovery of epistatic interactions and non-linear genetic effects. To overcome this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement machine learning models, including graph neural networks (GNNs) and gradient-boosted trees, trained on whole-genome sequencing data from 5,000 individuals with linked health records. Parallelized genome-wide association studies (GWAS) will be conducted using distributed computing frameworks to map loci influencing immune response variability. Additionally, agent-based simulations will model disease transmission dynamics within heterogeneous herds, incorporating stochastic environmental variables and host-pathogen interactions at scale. The computational workflow will utilize containerized pipelines for reproducibility, with an expected data throughput of 200 TB. Outcomes will include (1) predictive models linking genetic architecture to disease susceptibility, (2) optimized breeding strategies targeting resilience traits, and (3) open-source tools for large-scale agricultural genomics. By harnessing HPC capabilities, this work aims to reduce reliance on antimicrobial interventions while improving swine health outcomes, directly supporting sustainable livestock production. The requested resources will enable processing times reduced from weeks to days, facilitating rapid iteration critical for addressing emerging zoonotic threats.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
