These solvers will leverage GPU acceleration and distributed-memory architectures to handle meshes with >10^6 elements, enabling rapid evaluation of geometric variations under realistic operating conditions. Additionally, machine learning models will be trained on HPC-generated datasets to predict stress concentrations, deformation thresholds, and manufacturing tolerances, integrating these predictions directly into CAD/CADD software via API-based frameworks. The outcomes will include optimized algorithms for automated geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T) compliance, reduced computational overhead for multi-objective design optimization, and open-source templates for scalable simulation workflows. By bridging the gap between high-resolution simulation and practical drafting workflows, this work aims to enhance the precision of mechanical design processes, reduce prototyping costs, and support the adoption of additive manufacturing and other advanced production techniques. The requested HPC resources are critical to achieving the necessary scale and speed for these computationally intensive tasks, which cannot be feasibly executed on local workstations.
cip_title: Mechanical Drafting and Mechanical Drafting CAD/ CADD
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to develop working drawings and electronic simulations in support of mechanical and industrial engineers, and related professionals. Includes instruction in manufacturing materials and processes, mechanical drafting, electrode-mechanical drafting, basic metallurgy, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, blueprint reading, and technical communication.

abstract: This project seeks to address the computational challenges inherent in fitting complex Bayesian hierarchical models to large-scale spatial and temporal datasets, a critical bottleneck in modern statistical research. Such models are increasingly used in epidemiology, environmental science, and public policy to capture dependencies across multiple scales and integrate heterogeneous data sources. However, their implementation is hindered by the computational intensity of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, particularly when applied to high-dimensional parameter spaces and massive datasets. The research will develop and optimize scalable algorithms for Bayesian inference, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to parallelize MCMC sampling across multiple nodes, implement GPU-accelerated gradient-based variational inference, and exploit sparse matrix techniques for efficient handling of spatial covariance structures. Key computational innovations include hybrid sampling schemes that combine Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with adaptive Metropolis-Hastings steps, distributed memory parallelism for hierarchical model components, and memory-efficient data partitioning strategies. The project will validate these methods through case studies analyzing multi-decadal climate model outputs paired with satellite-derived environmental data, as well as epidemiological datasets tracking disease spread across urban networks. Expected outcomes include a publicly available open-source software package optimized for HPC environments, benchmarks demonstrating order-of-magnitude improvements in sampling efficiency for common model classes, and novel statistical insights into spatiotemporal processes underlying climate extremes and infectious disease transmission. By enabling the practical application of richly structured Bayesian models to real-world problems at unprecedented scales, this work will advance statistical methodology while providing actionable tools for interdisciplinary researchers grappling with complex, data-intensive challenges. The requested computing resources are essential for testing algorithmic scalability, conducting large-scale simulations, and ensuring reproducibility across diverse application domains.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in mathematics and statistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance interdisciplinary research on the cultural narratives and linguistic diversity of Appalachia through large-scale analysis of historical and contemporary textual, audio, and visual materials. Appalachia’s cultural heritage is richly documented in community archives, oral histories, folk music recordings, and regional literature, yet these resources remain understudied at scale due to their fragmented distribution and the technical challenges of processing multimodal, non-standardized data. The research problem centers on identifying patterns of cultural transmission, dialect evolution, and narrative themes across time and subregions, with a focus on underrepresented voices, including Indigenous and African American communities. Computational methods will include natural language processing (NLP) to analyze dialect features in transcribed oral histories, machine learning models to classify thematic elements in folk music lyrics, and geospatial mapping tools to visualize cultural data against socioeconomic and environmental datasets. HPC resources are critical for training custom NLP models on historical Appalachian English corpora, processing high-resolution audio files for ethnomusicological analysis, and managing iterative analysis of terabyte-scale digitized archives. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible digital repository of annotated cultural materials, interactive maps linking cultural trends to community resilience indicators, and novel methodologies for ethically engaged computational humanities in regional studies. This work will provide scholars and Appalachian communities with tools to trace cultural continuity amid socioeconomic change, inform language preservation efforts, and challenge homogenizing stereotypes through data-driven narratives. The project aligns with Appalachian Studies’ emphasis on community-based research by collaborating with regional archives and cultural organizations to prioritize open access and participatory design.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the history, sociology, culture, and economics of the Appalachian region of the United States. Includes instruction in contemporary issues in Appalachia, political economy of Appalachia, community-based research, ethnomusicology, and oral and written languages of Appalachia.

abstract: The accelerating impacts of climate change, habitat fragmentation, and invasive species necessitate advanced predictive tools to optimize conservation strategies for terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. This project seeks to develop a spatially explicit modeling framework to forecast wildlife population dynamics and habitat suitability under multiple environmental stressors, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to overcome current computational limitations. The research focuses on three interconnected challenges: (1) simulating fine-scale species-environment interactions across heterogeneous landscapes, (2) integrating genomic data to assess adaptive potential in climate-vulnerable species, and (3) evaluating the efficacy of proposed management interventions under diverse climate scenarios. Computational methods will combine agent-based models (ABMs) with machine learning approaches to analyze movement patterns, resource use, and genetic connectivity using multi-terabyte datasets from GPS collars, environmental sensors, and whole-genome sequencing. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of ensemble climate projections (CMIP6) at 1km resolution, nested within regional hydrological models to assess surface water availability for aquatic species. Expected outcomes include the identification of climate-resilient habitat corridors, genomic markers associated with thermal tolerance in keystone species, and decision-support tools for prioritizing restoration efforts. By quantifying trade-offs between conservation actions under uncertainty, this work will provide actionable strategies for maintaining biodiversity in managed wildlands and protected areas. The scale of spatiotemporal data integration and the need for real-time parameter optimization in adaptive management scenarios exceed the capabilities of local computing infrastructure, necessitating dedicated HPC allocation. This project directly supports the program’s mission to advance evidence-based wildlands management while training students in computational ecology techniques.
cip_title: Wildlife, Fish and Wildlands Science and Management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to conserve and manage wilderness areas and the flora, marine and aquatic life therein, and manage wildlife reservations and zoological/aquarium facilities for recreational, commercial, and ecological purposes. Includes instruction in wildlife biology, marine/aquatic biology, environmental science, freshwater and saltwater ecosystems, natural resources management and policy, outdoor recreation and parks management, the design and operation of natural and artificial wildlife habitats, applicable law and regulations, and related administrative and communications skills.

abstract: The increasing complexity of modern electrical and electronic systems necessitates advanced methodologies for predictive maintenance and failure analysis to minimize downtime and repair costs. Traditional diagnostic approaches often rely on reactive strategies or rule-based systems, which lack adaptability to dynamic operational conditions and heterogeneous equipment configurations. This project proposes the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework for real-time anomaly detection and prognostic evaluation in industrial-scale electrical systems. The research will leverage machine learning (ML) models trained on multi-modal sensor data—including thermal imaging, voltage/current signatures, and vibration metrics—to identify early-stage component degradation and predict failure modes. Computational workflows will integrate time-series analysis, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and graph-based representations of system interdependencies, optimized for parallel processing on HPC clusters. A key innovation involves simulating fault propagation across interconnected subsystems using agent-based modeling, which requires significant memory and compute resources to capture emergent behaviors in large networks. The project will utilize open-source datasets from industrial partners and synthetically generated failure scenarios to validate model generalizability. Anticipated outcomes include a scalable software toolkit for maintenance technicians, capable of recommending targeted repair actions and optimizing resource allocation. By reducing unplanned outages through data-driven insights, this work aims to advance the technical capabilities of maintenance programs in energy distribution, manufacturing, and telecommunications infrastructure. The HPC environment is critical for handling terabyte-scale datasets, accelerating hyperparameter tuning via distributed computing, and enabling near-real-time inference in field-deployable applications. Results will be disseminated through industry partnerships and open-access repositories to bridge gaps between computational research and applied maintenance practices.
cip_title: Electrical/ Electronics Maintenance and Repair Technologies/ Technicians, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in electrical and electronics equipment installation and repair technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Traditional building inspection methodologies often depend on manual evaluations and post-construction assessments, limiting their ability to predict structural vulnerabilities proactively. This project proposes the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework to model building performance under multifactorial stressors, enabling predictive inspection workflows. The research will utilize parallelized finite element analysis to simulate structural responses to seismic activity, thermal cycling, and material fatigue across diverse construction typologies. Machine learning models, trained on heterogeneous datasets encompassing decades of inspection reports, LiDAR scans, and environmental sensor data, will identify latent risk factors correlated with code violations or premature degradation. HPC resources are critical for processing terabyte-scale datasets and iterating complex multiphysics simulations that account for regional building code variations. The computational pipeline will automate compliance verification against evolving standards (e.g., International Building Code updates) while generating probabilistic failure forecasts for infrastructure portfolios. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source risk prioritization toolkit for inspectors, validated through case studies on hurricane-prone coastal structures and aging urban high-rises. By transforming inspection protocols from reactive checklists to predictive systems, this work aims to reduce construction-related accidents by 15-20% within a decade while optimizing maintenance budgets. The project further contributes to academic curricula by creating modular training modules on computational inspection techniques, bridging the gap between traditional trade skills and data science competencies in vocational education programs.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply industrial, labor, and governmental standards and laws to the oversight of construction projects and the maintenance of completed buildings and other structures. Includes instruction in construction processes and techniques, materials analysis, occupational safety and health, industry standards, building codes and specifications, blueprint interpretation, testing equipment and procedures, communication skills, accident investigation, and documentation.

abstract: The integration of multimodal clinical data for real-time prediction of patient deterioration in intensive care units (ICUs) remains a significant challenge in clinical informatics. Current predictive models often fail to synthesize high-frequency streaming data from electronic health records (EHRs), wearable sensors, and medical imaging, leading to delayed interventions. This project seeks to address this gap by developing a scalable deep learning framework optimized for high-performance computing (HPC) environments. The research will focus on aggregating heterogeneous data streams, including time-series vital signs, radiology images, and unstructured clinical notes, to predict critical events such as sepsis or cardiac arrest. Computational methods will involve hybrid architectures combining convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image analysis, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with attention mechanisms for temporal data, and transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) models for clinical text interpretation. Federated learning techniques will be implemented to train models across multiple institutions while preserving data privacy. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel processing of petabytes of data, hyperparameter optimization at scale, and real-time inference simulations. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for multimodal clinical data integration, validated predictive models with sub-hourly deterioration alerts, and benchmarks for federated learning efficiency in healthcare settings. This work aims to provide clinicians with actionable, timely insights to improve ICU outcomes while establishing computational best practices for privacy-preserving machine learning in clinical informatics. The requested resources are critical for managing the computational intensity of training deep learning models on multimodal datasets and ensuring the translational relevance of these tools in dynamic healthcare environments.
cip_definition: Research focused on Clinical Informatics

abstract: Endocrine and metabolic disorders, including type 2 diabetes, obesity, and thyroid dysfunction, exhibit complex molecular and physiological heterogeneity that complicates diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Current clinical classifications often fail to capture this variability, leading to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes. This project proposes a computational framework to integrate multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics) with clinical electronic health records (EHRs) to identify patient-specific molecular subtypes and predictive biomarkers for endocrine disorders. The primary challenge lies in analyzing high-dimensional datasets with nonlinear interactions across temporal and spatial scales, which demands advanced machine learning (ML) and scalable computational infrastructure. We will develop a hybrid deep learning model combining graph neural networks (GNNs) to model biological networks and transformer architectures to process longitudinal EHR data. This approach will be validated using a cohort of 15,000 patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid obesity from the NIH All of Us Research Program, with replication in thyroid disorder datasets. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to train these models on terabytes of raw sequencing data, perform hyperparameter optimization via Bayesian methods, and conduct in silico simulations of metabolic pathways perturbed by identified genetic variants. Expected outcomes include (1) novel stratification of endocrine disorders into mechanistically distinct subgroups, (2) predictive algorithms for treatment response leveraging federated learning across institutions, and (3) open-source tools for dynamic visualization of multi-omics-clinical interactions. The computational workflows will be containerized for reproducibility, with GPU-accelerated scaling tested on HPC clusters. By linking molecular signatures to real-world outcomes, this work aims to advance precision endocrinology, reduce trial-and-error prescribing, and identify high-risk patients for early intervention. Successful implementation will require sustained access to HPC resources capable of parallel processing, large-memory nodes for genome-wide association study (GWAS) meta-analyses, and high-throughput pipelines for metabolomic feature extraction.
cip_definition: Research on disorders of the internal (endocrine) glands such as the thyroid and adrenal glands, and to deal with disorders such as diabetes, metabolic and nutritional disorders, obesity, pituitary diseases, and menstrual and sexual problems. Requires prior completion of a residency program in internal medicine.

abstract: Dental prostheses require precise biomechanical compatibility to ensure long-term functionality and patient comfort, yet current design methodologies rely heavily on empirical techniques with limited predictive capability for material fatigue, interfacial stress distribution, and microbial adhesion. This project proposes a computational framework to optimize the design and fabrication of dental prostheses by integrating multiscale biomechanical modeling, machine learning-driven material optimization, and patient-specific oral microenvironment simulations. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to address the computational complexity of modeling heterogeneous materials (e.g., zirconia, polymers, alloys) at micron-scale resolutions, simulating dynamic occlusal forces over multiyear timelines, and analyzing microbial biofilm formation under variable salivary conditions. The research will employ finite element analysis (FEA) to map stress gradients in prostheses, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to evaluate material degradation pathways, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on clinical imaging data to predict anatomical fit. A novel aspect involves coupling these models with real-world sensor data from intraoral scanning devices to validate simulations against biomechanical wear patterns observed in prostheses retrieved from patients. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms to guide the selection of material compositions and geometric configurations that minimize interfacial failure risks, reduce iterative prototyping, and extend prosthesis lifespan. By establishing a computational pipeline tailored to dental laboratory workflows, this work aims to bridge the gap between traditional craft-based fabrication and data-driven precision manufacturing, ultimately enhancing clinical outcomes for patients requiring complex restorative interventions. The scale of parameter space exploration (e.g., material hybrids, occlusal load scenarios) necessitates HPC capabilities to achieve statistically robust results within feasible timeframes.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of dentists, to design and construct dental prostheses such as caps, crowns, bridges, dentures, splints, and orthodontic appliances. Includes instruction in dental anatomy, dental materials, ceramics technology, impressions, complete dentures, partial dentures, orthodontics, crowns and bridges, sculpture, bonding and assembly techniques, and equipment operation.

abstract: Medical office management faces growing complexity due to evolving regulatory requirements, dynamic patient scheduling demands, and the integration of heterogeneous data streams from electronic health records (EHRs), billing systems, and operational workflows. Current decision-support tools often rely on simplified heuristics that fail to capture the nonlinear interactions between administrative variables, leading to suboptimal resource allocation and operational inefficiencies. This project proposes the development of a high-resolution computational framework to model medical office operations as adaptive systems, with the goal of identifying context-sensitive strategies for staff scheduling, patient flow optimization, and compliance risk mitigation. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will implement agent-based modeling to simulate interactions between patients, providers, and administrative staff under diverse operational scenarios. The framework will integrate real-world datasets spanning appointment histories, EHR metadata, and staffing patterns, processed through graph neural networks to identify latent dependencies between operational parameters. Temporal convolution networks will be trained to predict bottlenecks in patient throughput, while reinforcement learning architectures will explore optimal policy adaptations under constraints such as budget limitations or emergent regulatory changes. Validation will occur through retrospective analysis of historical clinic performance data and prospective pilot testing in three outpatient facilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models capable of recommending dynamic staffing adjustments, automated identification of compliance vulnerabilities in billing practices, and scenario-testing interfaces for administrators. By bridging computational systems science with healthcare operations management, this work aims to establish a foundation for data-driven decision-making in medical administration, reducing operational costs by an estimated 12-18% in modeled environments while maintaining patient care quality standards. The computational infrastructure developed will serve as a template for scalable, adaptive management systems in medium-sized healthcare practices.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage the specialized business functions of a medical or clinical office. Includes instruction in business office operations, business and financial record-keeping, personnel supervision, medical and health care policy administration, conference planning, scheduling and coordination, public relations, and applicable law and regulations.

abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) results in complex, multifaceted disabilities that require interdisciplinary approaches to improve patient outcomes. Current clinical strategies for SCI management remain limited by incomplete understanding of injury heterogeneity, variable recovery trajectories, and the interplay between biological, biomechanical, and psychosocial factors. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to integrate multimodal datasets—including clinical records, neuroimaging, sensor-derived biomechanical data, and molecular profiling—into predictive models of functional recovery and treatment response. A key challenge lies in the high-dimensional integration of temporally dynamic data across scales, from cellular processes to patient-reported outcomes, necessitating advanced computational infrastructure. The research will employ machine learning frameworks, such as graph neural networks and ensemble methods, to identify biomarkers of neurological recovery and optimize personalized rehabilitation protocols. Concurrently, finite element modeling and computational fluid dynamics simulations will be applied to investigate cerebrospinal fluid dynamics post-injury, which may inform interventions for neuropathic pain and autonomic dysreflexia. These analyses require large-scale parallel processing capabilities and GPU-accelerated workloads to manage iterative model training and simulate multicompartmental biophysical systems. Expected outcomes include the development of open-source tools for SCI data integration, validated predictive algorithms for clinical deployment, and mechanistic insights into secondary injury cascades. By enabling real-time analysis of terabyte-scale datasets and computationally intensive simulations, the requested HPC resources will directly support translational advances in SCI medicine, including the design of adaptive clinical trials and patient-specific neuroprosthetic interfaces. This work aligns with national priorities to reduce long-term disability burdens through precision rehabilitation, offering a scalable computational foundation for future studies in neurotrauma recovery.
cip_definition: Research on how to address the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and management of traumatic spinal cord injury and non-traumatic etiologies of spinal cord dysfunction, including related medical, physical, psychological, and vocational disabilities and complications.

abstract: Clinical educators face significant challenges in analyzing complex, multimodal datasets generated from simulation-based training, competency assessments, and longitudinal evaluations of interprofessional education outcomes. Traditional analytical methods struggle to integrate high-dimensional data from diverse sources—including performance metrics, behavioral logs, and free-text feedback—limiting the ability to optimize training efficacy or personalize learning pathways. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing scalable computational models to identify patterns in educational effectiveness and learner progression across health professions specialties. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process terabytes of anonymized data from institutional learning management systems, virtual patient simulations, and competency assessments spanning medicine, nursing, and allied health disciplines. Machine learning approaches, including natural language processing for qualitative feedback analysis and graph neural networks for modeling skill acquisition trajectories, will be implemented. Parallelized algorithms will enable real-time analysis of simulation log files to correlate clinical decision-making patterns with post-training patient outcomes. A key innovation involves federated learning architectures to preserve data privacy while training models across multiple institutions. Expected outcomes include predictive frameworks for identifying at-risk learners, evidence-based guidelines for adaptive curriculum design, and open-source tools for benchmarking interprofessional competency development. By enabling large-scale, integrative analysis of educational data, this work will advance precision education strategies in health professions training, ultimately improving the scalability and equity of clinical instruction. The requested HPC resources are critical for managing distributed datasets, reducing model training times from weeks to days, and supporting the computational demands of multimodal artificial intelligence pipelines. Findings will directly inform accreditation standards and faculty development initiatives aimed at addressing systemic gaps in healthcare education.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on education and administration leadership skills for clinical educators across health professions and specialties. Includes instruction in academic leadership, assessment, clinical decision making, curriculum development, ethics, primary care education, program evaluation, research methods, and statistics.

abstract: Urban environments are increasingly shaped by the interplay of digital platforms and physical infrastructure, yet the socio-spatial implications of location-based social media (LBSM) on public space utilization remain poorly understood. This project addresses the critical gap in modeling how real-time, data-driven interactions on platforms like Foursquare and Pokémon GO influence collective behavior patterns, strain shared resources, and reshape equitable access to urban amenities. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we propose a multi-agent simulation framework integrating anonymized LBSM datasets, pedestrian mobility traces, and geospatial inventories of public infrastructure across three mid-sized cities. The computational model will employ graph neural networks (GNNs) to map dynamic preference cascades, coupled with reinforcement learning agents that adapt their movement patterns based on evolving social feedback loops. Spatial-temporal analytics will quantify emergent congestion hotspots and "digital deserts" where offline amenities fail to meet digitally amplified demand. By parallelizing sentiment analysis of 12 million geotagged posts across GPU clusters, the system will identify latent thresholds where virtual interactions trigger physical space saturation. Expected outcomes include a predictive toolkit for municipal planners to simulate platform-induced crowd dynamics during urban design processes, alongside policy frameworks for regulating locative media impacts on public space equity. This interdisciplinary approach advances computational urban science by bridging social media analytics with spatial justice theory, offering novel methodologies for managing hybrid digital-physical environments in smart cities.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of social science principles to the study of urban institutions and the forces influencing urban social and political life. Includes instruction in urban theory, the development and evolution of urban areas, urban sociology, principles of urban and social planning, and the politics and economics of urban government and services.

abstract: This project seeks to evaluate the economic efficiency of conservation policies under climate change uncertainty by developing an integrated modeling framework that combines dynamic econometric analysis, high-resolution climate projections, and large-scale optimization. Existing approaches often oversimplify spatial-temporal interactions between ecological systems and economic behavior, limiting their capacity to inform adaptive resource management. The research will address this gap by constructing a computationally intensive model that simulates decentralized decision-making by agricultural and industrial agents under shifting climate regimes, while incorporating feedbacks between regional biodiversity loss, land use change, and ecosystem service valuation. The computational methodology employs parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to quantify policy impacts across 10,000+ stochastic climate scenarios, Bayesian hierarchical models to analyze heterogeneous agent responses derived from satellite land cover data and microeconomic surveys, and evolutionary algorithms to identify Pareto-optimal resource allocation strategies. High-performance computing resources are essential for processing multi-terabyte environmental datasets (including NOAA climate records and ESA Sentinel-2 imagery), solving high-dimensional dynamic optimization problems with non-convex constraints, and running ensemble projections at 1km² resolution across three major U.S. watersheds. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible toolkit for comparing the cost-effectiveness of market-based conservation instruments (e.g., habitat banking, precision irrigation subsidies) under varying climate pathways, with explicit quantification of equity-efficiency trade-offs. Results will advance coupled human-environment systems modeling through novel integration of stochastic dominance analysis and spatially explicit biophysical thresholds, providing actionable insights for agencies managing climate-resilient resource allocation. The computational framework will be designed for scalability to global biodiversity hotspots, with intermediate outputs peer-reviewed in environmental economics journals and presented to the USDA and EPA through policy briefs.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of economic concepts and methods to the analysis of issues such as air and water pollution, land use planning, waste disposal, invasive species and pest control, conservation policies, and related environmental problems. Includes instruction in cost-benefit analysis, environmental impact assessment, evaluation and assessment of alternative resource management strategies, policy evaluation and monitoring, and descriptive and analytic tools for studying how environmental developments affect the economic system.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance decision-support frameworks for next-generation military command, control, and intelligence operations. Modern multi-domain operations generate vast, heterogeneous data streams—from satellite imagery and sensor telemetry to unstructured human-generated reports—that challenge traditional analytical workflows. Current systems struggle to integrate these datasets in real time while accounting for adversarial deception tactics, resource constraints, and rapidly evolving mission parameters. To address this gap, we propose developing an adaptive computational architecture combining agent-based modeling, graph-based anomaly detection, and reinforcement learning (RL) to simulate contested information environments and optimize decision pathways. The project will employ parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to model probabilistic outcomes of command choices under varying threat scenarios, while transformer-based natural language processing will automate the extraction of tacit insights from unstructured intelligence documents. A key innovation involves coupling these components through a dynamic knowledge graph that updates in near real time, enabling HPC-powered scenario testing to identify vulnerabilities in proposed strategies before deployment. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable framework for simulating multi-echelon command decisions under asymmetric information conditions, (2) quantifiable metrics for assessing the resilience of proposed courses of action against adversarial counter-strategies, and (3) open-source tools for visualizing decision trade-offs across temporal, spatial, and organizational dimensions. By enabling rapid iteration through complex what-if scenarios, this work aims to reduce cognitive overload in high-stakes environments while maintaining human oversight. The computational demands—particularly the need for distributed training of RL agents across thousands of concurrent simulations and real-time fusion of terabyte-scale sensor data—necessitate specialized HPC infrastructure. Successful implementation will provide a foundation for enhancing interoperability in joint operations and inform future investments in AI-assisted command systems.
cip_title: Intelligence, Command Control and Information Operations, Other (MILITARY)
cip_definition: Any instructional program in intelligence, command control and information operations, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The dynamical evolution of planetary systems is governed by complex gravitational interactions that shape orbital architectures over billion-year timescales. However, current models struggle to reconcile observed exoplanet systems—many exhibiting tightly packed configurations, resonant chains, or high eccentricities—with formation theories. This project seeks to address this gap by performing high-resolution N-body simulations of planetary system evolution, incorporating both internal gravitational perturbations and external perturbations from stellar clusters. The research will utilize the REBOUND code with the IAS15 adaptive integrator to model systems with up to 20 interacting bodies across 1–100 Myr timescales. Key challenges include resolving close encounters, maintaining numerical stability during chaotic interactions, and statistically sampling parameter space for initial conditions consistent with protoplanetary disk models. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential due to the O(n²) scaling of gravitational calculations and the need for ensemble simulations across 10^4 parameter combinations. Each simulation requires ~500 GB of memory for phase-space tracking and ~8 hours on 256 cores for a 10 Myr integration. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of stability criteria for compact multi-planet systems, (2) quantification of stellar cluster tidal effects on planetary eccentricity distribution, and (3) publicly released simulation datasets for comparative exoplanet studies. Results will directly inform interpretation of JWST transit spectra and ESA’s PLATO mission data by linking present-day observations to formation histories. This work advances fundamental understanding of how gravitational physics shapes planetary systems, with applications to habitability studies and population synthesis models.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of planets, small objects, and related gravitational systems. Includes instruction in the structure and composition of planetary surfaces and interiors, planetary atmospheres, satellites, orbital mechanics, asteroids and comets, solar system evolution and dynamics, planetary evolution, gravitational physics, and radiation physics.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to assess landslide susceptibility in tectonically active regions, with a focus on improving infrastructure resilience and site evaluation practices. Current methods for landslide prediction often rely on simplified geotechnical parameters or static geological maps, which inadequately capture dynamic interactions between hydrological processes, seismic activity, and heterogeneous subsurface materials. To address this, we propose a high-resolution, multiphysics framework integrating 3D finite element modeling of slope stability, machine learning-driven soil property estimation, and probabilistic seismic triggering scenarios. The computational workflow will process terabytes of geospatial data, including LiDAR-derived topography, InSAR deformation records, and regional borehole logs, to parameterize models at meter-scale resolution across 100+ km² study areas. High-performance computing resources are essential to execute Monte Carlo simulations quantifying uncertainty in failure thresholds under climate-driven precipitation extremes and earthquake recurrence intervals. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible risk assessment toolkit for engineers and a novel database correlating lithological heterogeneity with slope failure mechanisms. By enabling real-time updates of hazard maps during extreme weather events, this work directly supports the design of adaptive transportation infrastructure and improves construction site selection protocols in geologically complex terrains. The scalability of the framework will be validated across case studies in the Pacific Northwest and Himalayan regions, with potential applications to natural resource corridor planning and post-disaster recovery strategies.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and geological principles to the analysis and evaluation of engineering problems, including the geological evaluation of construction sites, the analysis of geological forces acting on structures and systems, the analysis of potential natural resource recovery sites, and applied research on geological phenomena.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of ocean-atmosphere coupling processes that drive tropical climate variability and extreme weather events under anthropogenic warming. A critical knowledge gap persists in modeling mesoscale ocean eddies and their cascading impacts on atmospheric convection, cloud feedbacks, and heat redistribution—processes poorly resolved in current-generation Earth system models (ESMs). To address this, we propose high-resolution coupled simulations using the Community Earth System Model (CESM) at an unprecedented 0.1° ocean/0.25° atmosphere resolution, explicitly resolving eddy-driven heat transport and air-sea interactions at storm-resolving scales. The computational workflow will leverage GPU-accelerated components of the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) framework optimized for high-performance computing (HPC) architectures. Key innovations include a multi-scale nesting approach to isolate eddy feedback mechanisms and machine learning-based parameterization of subgrid-scale cloud microphysics trained against ARM observational data. Simulations will span 50 model years under CMIP6 SSP2-4.5 forcing, requiring 8 million core-hours on a tier-2 HPC cluster to generate 3 PB of output data. Expected outcomes include (1) quantification of eddy-mediated ocean heat uptake efficiency, (2) improved representation of Madden-Julian Oscillation dynamics in warming scenarios, and (3) uncertainty reduction in projected tropical cyclone intensification rates. Results will directly inform the 7th IPCC Assessment Report by constraining climate sensitivity tied to ocean mixing processes. The resource request supports development of an open-source diagnostics package for eddy-resolving climate model intercomparison, fostering community-wide advances in high-resolution climate prediction. This work bridges critical gaps between oceanographic small-scale physics and global climate response, with implications for coastal resilience planning and mitigation strategy evaluation.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the climate system of the earth with emphasis on the physical, dynamical, and chemical interactions of the atmosphere, ocean, land, ice, and the terrestrial and marine biospheres. Includes instruction in biology, chemistry, climate analysis, climate change adaptation/mitigation, climate policy, ecology, energy development, environmental impacts, marine chemistry, meteorology, and oceanography.

abstract: Semiconductor manufacturing involves complex physical and chemical processes that require precise control to optimize yield, performance, and cost. A critical challenge lies in modeling multiphysics phenomena—such as thermal stress during rapid thermal processing (RTP), plasma dynamics in etching, and defect propagation in crystalline structures—which are computationally intensive and influence device reliability at scale. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop multiscale simulations that bridge atomic-level interactions with continuum-scale manufacturing processes. The research will focus on two interconnected aims: (1) simulating defect formation in silicon wafers under varying process conditions using molecular dynamics (MD) and finite element analysis (FEA), and (2) training machine learning (ML) models to predict optimal process parameters for minimizing defects while maximizing throughput. The computational workflow will integrate open-source tools (LAMMPS, OpenFOAM) with custom Python-based ML pipelines to analyze terabyte-scale datasets of process variables, material properties, and real-time sensor data. HPC resources are essential to handle the parallelized MD simulations of nanoscale interactions (10^6–10^9 atoms) and the iterative optimization of ML hyperparameters across thousands of experimental permutations. Expected outcomes include validated models for predicting thermal gradient-induced wafer warpage, a framework for coupling ML with multiphysics simulations, and a publicly accessible dataset of process-structure-property relationships. These results will directly inform the design of next-generation semiconductor fabrication protocols, reducing trial-and-error experimentation in industrial settings. By elucidating the interplay between process variables and defect mechanics, this work aims to advance foundational knowledge in semiconductor manufacturing technology while providing students with hands-on training in computational modeling and data-driven materials engineering. The project aligns with national priorities to strengthen domestic semiconductor production capabilities through innovation in advanced manufacturing technologies.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills to operate and monitor equipment for the fabrication of semiconductors or microchips from silicon wafers, and to troubleshoot, maintain, and repair the specialized equipment used in this process. Includes instruction in AC and DC circuits, digital fundamentals, solid state devices, manufacturing processes, vacuum principles and technology, industrial electronics, quality assurance, and semiconductor manufacturing technology.

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing computational demands of simulating and optimizing civil infrastructure designs in complex geological environments, a critical challenge in civil drafting and engineering CAD/CADD workflows. Current software tools struggle to efficiently model large-scale infrastructure systems—such as water distribution networks or transportation corridors—while integrating high-resolution geological, hydrological, and seismic data. These limitations hinder the ability to predict system resilience under dynamic stressors like earthquakes or climate-induced soil instability. To overcome this, we propose developing a scalable computational framework using high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable multi-physics simulations that couple finite element analysis, geospatial data processing, and automated drafting parameter optimization. The project will leverage parallelized algorithms to distribute tasks across HPC nodes, accelerating iterative design testing and sensitivity analyses. Key computational components include GPU-accelerated rendering for 3D geological mapping, machine learning models to predict material stress thresholds from historical survey data, and parametric scripting to automate CADD blueprint revisions. By integrating these methods, the framework will reduce simulation runtime for large infrastructure projects from weeks to days while improving precision in risk assessment. Outcomes will include open-source CADD workflow modules tailored for academic training and a case study validating the approach on a regional stormwater management system with variable soil composition. This work will advance computational drafting methodologies, support climate-resilient infrastructure design, and provide students with hands-on experience in HPC-aided civil engineering workflows, bridging gaps between traditional drafting techniques and modern computational geotechnics.
cip_title: Civil Drafting and Civil Engineering CAD/ CADD
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to develop working drawing and electronic simulations in support of civil engineers, geological engineers, and related professionals. Includes instruction in basic civil engineering principles, geological and seismographic mapping, machine drafting, computer-aided drafting (CAD), pipe drafting, survey interpretation, and blueprint reading.

abstract: This research project seeks to optimize dynamic customer engagement strategies in tourism and travel services through the integration of real-time behavioral analytics and hyper-personalized marketing simulations. The tourism sector faces challenges in balancing operational efficiency with individualized customer experiences, particularly as fluctuating demand, seasonal trends, and heterogeneous traveler preferences strain traditional marketing models. Current approaches often rely on static segmentation or heuristic-based decision-making, limiting responsiveness to real-time data streams from booking platforms, social media, and IoT-enabled hotel systems. To address this gap, we propose developing an adaptive computational framework that combines agent-based modeling (ABM) with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to simulate multi-channel customer interactions at scale. The ABM component will emulate traveler decision pathways influenced by demographic variables, situational constraints, and real-time pricing signals, while DRL agents will iteratively optimize promotional offers, room allocation policies, and service bundling strategies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for processing high-dimensional datasets from 12+ tourism partners (encompassing ~2.3 million annual transactions) and executing parallelized simulations across diverse market scenarios. The computational workflow will leverage GPU-accelerated graph neural networks to model cross-customer influence networks and containerized microservices for A/B testing virtual campaigns. Expected outcomes include a predictive dashboard for dynamic pricing elasticity thresholds and evidence-based guidelines for automating personalized upselling interventions. By quantifying trade-offs between operational resource allocation and customer lifetime value metrics, this work aims to establish scalable decision-support tools for mid-tier hospitality businesses lacking enterprise-grade analytics infrastructure. The project will contribute methodological innovations in applying swarm intelligence paradigms to service operations while addressing sector-specific challenges in perishable inventory management and experience-driven consumer behavior.
cip_title: Tourism and Travel Services Marketing Operations
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to provide direct retail services to hotel and motel clients and customers in a variety of settings. Includes instruction in the principles of hotel/motel operations, customer sales and assistance operations and techniques, telephone operations, and basic office management.

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing material performance and structural integrity in upholstered products through advanced computational modeling. Traditional upholstery design relies heavily on empirical testing, which is resource-intensive and limited in its ability to predict long-term material behavior under dynamic mechanical, thermal, and environmental stresses. To overcome these limitations, we propose a computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate multiscale interactions between upholstery materials—such as foams, textiles, and springs—and their operational environments. The research will focus on two primary objectives: (1) developing finite element analysis (FEA) models to predict stress distribution, fatigue, and deformation in complex upholstered assemblies (e.g., furniture, automotive seats), and (2) employing machine learning algorithms to correlate material composition with performance metrics like durability, comfort, and thermal regulation. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations will further investigate degradation mechanisms in synthetic fibers and cushioning materials under repeated loading cycles. By integrating these approaches, the project aims to establish predictive models that reduce reliance on physical prototyping, accelerate design iterations, and enhance sustainability through data-driven material optimization. The computational workflows will be validated against experimental datasets collected from industry partners, ensuring practical relevance. Anticipated outcomes include open-access simulation tools tailored for upholstery applications, a materials database linking microstructural properties to macroscopic performance, and design guidelines for improving product lifespans. This work represents a transformative step in modernizing upholstery practices by bridging craft-based expertise with computational engineering, with potential impacts on manufacturing efficiency, waste reduction, and ergonomic innovation. The requested HPC resources are essential for handling the high-resolution simulations and parameter space exploration required to capture nonlinear material behaviors at scale.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to install springs, filling, padding, covering and finishing on items such as furniture, automobile seats, caskets, mattresses, and bedsprings.

abstract: Hospice and palliative care research faces a critical challenge in predicting patient-centered outcomes due to the complex interplay of biological, psychosocial, and symptom-related variables in advanced illness. Existing prognostic models often lack the granularity and scalability required to inform personalized care plans, particularly for patients with multi-morbidity or rapidly evolving symptoms. This project proposes to develop a machine learning framework to analyze multi-modal clinical data—including electronic health records (EHRs), longitudinal symptom reports, genomic markers of pain sensitivity, and caregiver narratives—to predict trajectories of functional decline, symptom burden, and quality of life in patients receiving palliative care. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process terabytes of structured and unstructured data, train deep neural networks on temporal patterns across heterogeneous datasets, and perform Bayesian optimization for dynamic risk stratification. Computational workflows will integrate natural language processing (NLP) for extracting semantic features from clinician notes and patient-reported outcomes, federated learning to preserve privacy across six participating hospice institutions, and ensemble methods to address class imbalance in rare clinical events. The resulting models will be validated against prospective outcomes in a cohort of 2,300 patients and deployed as open-source tools for real-time decision support. This work aims to advance the precision of palliative care interventions by identifying subpopulations at risk for under-managed symptoms, optimizing the timing of hospice transitions, and elucidating biological signatures associated with end-of-life experiences. The requested HPC allocation will enable iterative model refinement at scale, reducing training times for 3D convolutional networks analyzing functional MRI correlates of delirium from weeks to days. Outcomes will directly inform clinical trial designs for personalized pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic therapies while establishing computational infrastructure for collaborative palliative care research.
cip_definition: Research focused on Hospice and Palliative Medicine

abstract: Public horticulture initiatives increasingly face challenges in optimizing plant performance and community engagement within dynamic urban environments, where complex interactions between environmental variables, plant physiology, and human behavior limit predictive capabilities. Traditional experimental approaches struggle to disentangle these multidimensional relationships at scales relevant to real-world applications. This project proposes an integrated computational framework to model plant-environment-community systems, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance decision-making in public horticulture. The research will focus on developing agent-based models (ABMs) that simulate plant growth responses to microclimate variability and parallelized machine learning algorithms to analyze community engagement patterns from longitudinal survey data. Key objectives include parameterizing plant physiology models using hyperspectral imaging datasets, validating climate resilience predictions across diverse horticultural taxa, and identifying socioeconomic drivers of public interaction with urban green spaces. Computational workflows will integrate soil sensor networks, LiDAR-derived 3D canopy structures, and citizen science observations from partner botanical gardens. The HPC infrastructure will enable ensemble simulations assessing thousands of scenario combinations, from irrigation optimization under drought stress to educational program efficacy across demographic groups. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for predicting plant performance in public landscapes, evidence-based frameworks for outreach program design, and multi-criteria optimization pipelines for urban horticulture planning. By quantifying relationships between biological requirements, environmental constraints, and human behavioral factors at unprecedented resolution, this work will provide critical insights for sustaining urban plant ecosystems while maximizing their educational and social value. The computational resources will directly support graduate training in data-driven horticultural science, bridging disciplinary gaps between plant biology, computational modeling, and community-centered design.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
detailed_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences nec
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on combining traditional horticulture and public education and outreach. Includes instruction in botany, soil science, plant science, agricultural economics, leadership, and business.

abstract: Educational evaluation research faces persistent challenges in modeling complex, multilevel interventions and their heterogeneous effects across diverse student populations. Traditional statistical methods often struggle to account for high-dimensional contextual data, longitudinal interactions, and non-linear relationships that characterize real-world educational programs. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing and validating computational models capable of simulating large-scale educational interventions while incorporating granular data on student demographics, institutional characteristics, and community factors. The research will employ machine learning techniques—including Bayesian additive regression trees and neural networks—to analyze existing longitudinal datasets from statewide K-12 assessments paired with socioeconomic indicators. Concurrently, agent-based modeling will simulate intervention scenarios across virtual student populations derived from census microdata. These computational approaches require high-performance resources to manage three critical tasks: (1) processing terabyte-scale administrative records with privacy-preserving federated learning architectures, (2) running parallelized Monte Carlo simulations for policy scenario testing, and (3) training ensemble models that integrate both observational and simulated data streams. The requested computing infrastructure will enable analysis at unprecedented spatial granularity (school-district level) while maintaining individual student-level fidelity through synthetic data techniques. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for dynamic treatment effect estimation in educational settings, validated against experimental studies from three current federal grant projects. This work aims to advance evaluation methodology by producing tools that better capture implementation variability and long-term intervention effects, directly informing resource allocation decisions in Title I programs and special education services. Results will be disseminated through computational education research networks and the National Center for Education Evaluation, with particular emphasis on reducing bias in predictive models used for at-risk student identification.
detailed_field: Educational assessment, evaluation, and research methods
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and procedures for generating information about educational programs, personnel and methods, and the analysis of such information for planning purposes. Includes instruction in evaluation theory, evaluation research design and planning, administering evaluations and related data collection activities, data reporting requirements, data analysis and interpretation, and related economic and policy issues.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing instructional strategies in STEM education by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model and analyze the efficacy of integrated, technology-enhanced learning environments. Despite growing emphasis on interdisciplinary STEM curricula, educators lack robust frameworks to predict how specific pedagogical approaches—such as project-based learning or adaptive educational technologies—affect the development of critical thinking and problem-solving skills in PreK-12 students. Current evaluation methods often rely on static assessments, which fail to capture the dynamic, non-linear interactions between instructional design, student engagement, and learning outcomes. To bridge this gap, we propose a computational study combining agent-based modeling, machine learning, and large-scale data analytics. The research will simulate classroom dynamics using anonymized longitudinal datasets (e.g., student performance metrics, interaction logs from digital learning platforms, and teacher feedback) to identify patterns in skill acquisition and knowledge transfer. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of multimodal data streams, training predictive models to forecast the impact of variables such as lesson sequencing, real-time feedback mechanisms, and collaborative learning structures. Additionally, we will employ natural language processing to analyze qualitative inputs, such as student reflections and teacher journals, enriching quantitative models with contextual insights. Outcomes will include a validated computational framework for designing adaptive STEM curricula, actionable recommendations for scaling effective teaching practices, and open-source tools to help educators visualize the projected outcomes of pedagogical choices. By elucidating the causal relationships between instructional methods and student competencies, this work aims to advance evidence-based strategies for STEM education, ultimately fostering equitable, data-driven teacher leadership and improving readiness in STEM fields for diverse learners.
cip_title: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) Educational Methods
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to connect education practices with scientific, engineering, and mathematical principles for PreK-12 students. Includes instruction in critical thinking, curriculum and instruction, history of STEM education, integrating STEM across curricula, learning sciences and technology, STEM education methods, and teacher leadership in STEM education.

abstract: This research project seeks to address inefficiencies in urban public transportation systems by developing a computational framework to optimize multimodal network design and dynamic resource allocation under fluctuating demand. Public transit agencies face challenges in balancing operational costs, environmental impact, and service quality, particularly as cities integrate emerging mobility technologies (e.g., ride-sharing, microtransit) with traditional fixed-route systems. Existing planning tools often lack the scalability to model city-scale networks or the flexibility to account for real-time disruptions and behavioral shifts. The project will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement a multi-objective optimization model that simultaneously evaluates infrastructure investments, fleet deployment strategies, and pricing policies across transportation modes. Agent-based simulations will capture traveler decision-making patterns using synthetic populations derived from census data, GPS traces, and transit smart card records. Machine learning techniques will be applied to historical datasets to predict demand variability under different economic and environmental scenarios. Computational experiments will focus on metropolitan regions with documented last-mile connectivity gaps and congestion bottlenecks. The HPC environment is critical for running parallelized simulations across thousands of scenario permutations, enabling sensitivity analyses of factors such as energy costs, equity constraints, and carbon emission targets. Expected outcomes include a decision support toolkit for transit agencies to evaluate trade-offs between capital expenditures, service frequency adjustments, and technology adoption timelines. Results will advance academic understanding of scalability challenges in mobility system modeling while providing actionable insights for public-private partnership structures in transportation management. This work directly aligns with transportation policy innovation goals in business administration by quantifying risk-mitigation strategies for large-scale infrastructure projects.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory, policy, law, and practices required to administrate and operate public transportation facilities, networks, services, and systems. Includes instruction in demand analysis and forecasting, environmental planning, facilities design and construction, geographic information systems (GIS), logistics, multi- and intermodal transportation systems, project management, public administration, public policy, transportation economics, transportation law, transportation operations, transportation systems, and transportation technologies.

abstract: Medical education faces increasing complexity in delivering effective training that integrates rapidly evolving clinical knowledge, interdisciplinary collaboration, and competency-based assessments. Traditional approaches to curriculum design and evaluation often rely on limited datasets or qualitative feedback, which may fail to capture the dynamic interactions between educational interventions, learner performance, and long-term clinical outcomes. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing computational models to simulate, analyze, and optimize medical education strategies using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. We propose a multi-modal approach combining machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), and network analysis to evaluate large-scale datasets from medical student assessments, residency training logs, electronic health records (EHRs), and faculty feedback. Computational workflows will model the impact of curricular changes on skill acquisition, identify latent biases in assessment tools, and predict downstream effects on clinical decision-making. HPC resources are essential for processing terabytes of structured and unstructured data, training deep neural networks on longitudinal performance metrics, and running parallel simulations of hypothetical curriculum designs. Key outcomes include actionable insights into optimizing adaptive learning pathways, reducing disparities in competency evaluations, and enhancing retention of high-stakes clinical knowledge. By bridging gaps between educational theory and data-driven practice, this work aims to establish a scalable framework for iterative curriculum improvement in academic medical centers. The requested computing infrastructure will enable rapid iteration of models that would otherwise be computationally intractable, directly supporting the translation of research findings into real-world medical training environments.
cip_definition: Research on how to teach deliver, design, and evaluate courses and curricula for medical students, residents, and faculty.

abstract: This project seeks to address the computational challenges of analyzing complex, high-dimensional social science datasets to model societal inequality dynamics. Traditional statistical methods often struggle with the scale, heterogeneity, and interdependencies inherent in modern social data, such as longitudinal surveys, administrative records, and geospatial indicators. The research aims to develop scalable Bayesian hierarchical models with spatial-temporal components to quantify how economic, demographic, and policy factors interact across multiple scales (individual, community, regional). A key innovation is the integration of stochastic processes and non-parametric techniques to handle missing data, sampling biases, and nonlinear relationships common in social datasets. The computational approach relies on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and variational inference algorithms, optimized for parallel processing on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters. This enables efficient sampling from posterior distributions with millions of parameters while accounting for complex covariance structures and autocorrelation. The project will utilize open-source tools (e.g., Stan, NumPyro) adapted for GPU-accelerated workflows to reduce runtime for large-scale simulations. Expected outcomes include (1) publicly available software for social scientists to fit interpretable inequality models without sacrificing computational feasibility, (2) granular estimates of policy impacts on inequality trends across diverse populations, and (3) methodological advances in regression-based techniques for sparse, imbalanced social data. By leveraging HPC resources, this work will overcome memory and runtime barriers that limit conventional statistical analyses, providing empirically grounded insights into the drivers of inequality. Results will inform targeted interventions and advance quantitative social science methodology through reproducible case studies using census microdata, labor force statistics, and global development indicators.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the social scientific applications of relationships between groups of measurements, and similarities and differences, using probability theory and techniques derived from it. Includes instruction in quantitative social science methodologies, the principles in probability theory, binomial distribution, regression analysis, standard deviation, stochastic processes, non-parametric statistics, sampling theory, and statistical techniques.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in Mormon Studies by analyzing complex patterns in Latter-day Saint theological discourse and community dynamics. The research problem centers on the need to systematically examine large-scale, unstructured textual and cultural datasets—including digitized sermons, doctrinal commentaries, and archival records—to identify shifts in theological emphasis, socioreligious adaptation, and the interplay between doctrinal authority and lived practice across time. Traditional qualitative methods face limitations in processing these datasets due to their volume, temporal scope, and multivariate nature. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to perform semantic clustering, sentiment analysis, and topic modeling on corpora spanning 19th-century foundational texts to contemporary digital media. Concurrently, agent-based modeling will simulate decision-making processes in historical and modern Mormon communities, testing hypotheses about cultural transmission and resilience under external pressures. HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based models on domain-specific language, optimizing hyperparameters for historical text analysis, and running large-scale simulations with dynamic socioreligious variables. Expected outcomes include the identification of previously unrecognized doctrinal development trajectories, quantitative frameworks for assessing cultural adaptation strategies, and open-access tools tailored to religious studies scholarship. This work will contribute to broader debates in the philosophy of religion regarding innovation within tradition and offer methodological advancements in applying computational methods to theological analysis. By bridging digital humanities and religious studies, the project aims to establish scalable, reproducible approaches for studying religious systems as dynamic, data-rich phenomena.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on beliefs, practices, culture, and history of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormon). Includes instruction in Mormon culture, history, literature, philosophy, sociology, and theology.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize dynamic resource allocation in multi-hospital networks under uncertainty, addressing critical inefficiencies in health system operations. Current approaches to resource sharing—such as staff, equipment, and specialty care access—often rely on static, facility-centric models ill-equipped to handle fluctuating demand, supply chain disruptions, or emergent public health crises. Using high-performance computing (HPC), we propose an agent-based simulation platform that integrates real-time data streams (e.g., patient volume, staff availability, supply inventories) with predictive analytics to model interdependencies across hospitals. The platform will employ reinforcement learning algorithms to iteratively optimize resource redistribution strategies while balancing cost, equity, and operational constraints. Computational challenges include scaling neural networks to simulate thousands of concurrent decision points across heterogeneous institutions and validating models against synthetic crisis scenarios (e.g., natural disasters, pandemic surges). By leveraging GPU-accelerated clusters, we aim to reduce simulation runtime for system-wide decision trees from weeks to hours, enabling rapid scenario testing. Expected outcomes include actionable protocols for adaptive resource sharing, quantified trade-off analyses for policymakers, and open-source tools to simulate region-specific crises. This work bridges computational scalability gaps in health administration, offering a paradigm shift from reactive to proactive resource management in complex care ecosystems. Success would directly inform national guidelines for health system resilience, reducing bottlenecks in care delivery during high-stakes scenarios.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to develop, plan, and manage health care operations and services within health care facilities and across health care systems. Includes instruction in planning, business management, financial management, public relations, human resources management, health care systems operation and management, health care resource allocation and policy making, health law and regulations, and applications to specific types of health care services.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in optimizing healthcare delivery systems through advanced computational modeling and data analytics. The research problem centers on the inefficiencies in resource allocation, operational workflows, and policy evaluation within complex healthcare environments, which are exacerbated by dynamic patient populations, fluctuating demand, and heterogeneous regulatory landscapes. Traditional analytical methods often fail to capture the interdependencies among these factors, limiting the ability to predict outcomes or design scalable interventions. To overcome these limitations, this study will develop large-scale simulation models integrating agent-based modeling, discrete-event simulation, and machine learning techniques to analyze multi-source data, including electronic health records, insurance claims, and public health datasets. These models will simulate scenarios such as hospital capacity planning, workforce distribution, emergency response coordination, and the impact of reimbursement policies on service accessibility. HPC resources are essential to manage the computational intensity of parallelized simulations, real-time optimization of stochastic parameters, and training predictive algorithms on terabyte-scale datasets. Expected outcomes include actionable insights into cost-effective resource allocation strategies, predictive tools for mitigating service bottlenecks, and evidence-based frameworks for evaluating the equity and sustainability of health policies. The results will directly inform healthcare administrators and policymakers, enabling data-driven decisions to enhance system resilience, reduce disparities, and improve population health outcomes. This work aligns with the Health Services Administration program’s emphasis on integrating management, policy, and operational analytics to advance healthcare delivery.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of policy analysis, public administration, business management, and communications to the planning and management of health services delivery systems in the public and private sectors, and prepares individuals to function as health services administrators and managers. Includes instruction in health systems planning, public health organization and management, pubic health policy formulation and analysis, finance, business and operations management, economics of health care, organizational and health communications, marketing, human resources management, and public health law and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing the integration of autonomous vehicle fleets into mixed urban traffic systems, addressing critical gaps in real-time decision-making and energy efficiency. Current approaches to autonomous ground transportation lack scalable models that account for dynamic interactions between human-operated vehicles, infrastructure constraints, and variable energy demands under real-world conditions. To address this, we propose a multiscale simulation environment combining agent-based traffic modeling, vehicle-to-infrastructure communication protocols, and predictive energy management algorithms. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to execute parallelized simulations of urban networks at varying temporal and spatial resolutions, incorporating machine learning techniques to refine decision policies through reinforcement learning.
