The central challenge lies in optimizing complex building systems for energy efficiency, structural resilience, and spatial functionality under dynamic environmental conditions—a task requiring iterative analysis of multi-physics interactions that exceed the capabilities of conventional architectural software. Current workflows in architectural practice rely on compartmentalized simulations (e.g., static thermal models or isolated structural analyses), leading to suboptimal solutions when addressing interconnected design parameters. This project proposes a computational framework that unifies parametric modeling, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), finite element analysis (FEA), and machine learning-driven optimization into a cohesive HPC pipeline. By parallelizing simulations across climate zones, material properties, and usage scenarios, the system will enable rapid exploration of design alternatives that balance competing priorities such as embodied carbon reduction, passive heating/cooling performance, and adaptive reuse potential. Key computational methods include GPU-accelerated physics engines for real-time feedback, graph-based optimization algorithms to navigate high-dimensional design spaces, and uncertainty quantification to assess robustness against climate variability. The research will utilize existing architectural datasets and generate new synthetic training data for predictive models. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for scalable architectural performance analysis, validated through case studies on mixed-use urban structures in climatically diverse regions. By democratizing access to HPC-driven design exploration, this work aims to bridge the gap between academic research and practical architectural workflows, empowering practitioners to create buildings that proactively respond to environmental challenges while maintaining aesthetic and functional rigor. Success will be measured by computational efficiency gains over industry-standard tools, quantitative improvements in energy performance predictions, and the toolkit’s adoption in pedagogical settings for architectural technology programs.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to assist architects in developing plans and related documentation and in performing architectural office services. Includes instruction in architectural drafting, computer-assisted drafting and design, construction methods and materials, environmental systems, building codes and standards, structural principles, cost estimation, planning documentation, visual communication skills, display production, and architectural office management.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize metal fabrication processes by simulating thermal-mechanical interactions during welding and cutting operations, with the goal of minimizing structural defects and improving material efficiency. Metal fabricators face persistent challenges in controlling heat-affected zones (HAZs), residual stresses, and dimensional inaccuracies in high-precision components, particularly when working with advanced alloys or complex geometries. Traditional trial-and-error methods to mitigate these issues are time-intensive and resource-heavy, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven approach combining finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) to model multi-physics interactions during fabrication. High-resolution simulations will capture transient thermal gradients, phase transformations, and stress distributions in ferrous and non-ferrous metals under varying toolpaths, shielding gas flows, and energy inputs. A parametric ML model will then identify optimal process parameters to reduce warping and microcracking while maintaining production speed. The computational workload necessitates HPC resources due to the scale of 3D meshing requirements (10⁶–10⁷ elements), coupled multi-physics solvers, and iterative optimization loops across thousands of parameter combinations. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source simulation toolkit tailored for vocational training programs, predictive guidelines for minimizing post-fabrication machining, and a database linking material properties to process settings. By integrating computational modeling into metal fabrication workflows, this project aims to bridge gaps between theoretical metallurgy and shop-floor practices, reducing material waste by an estimated 15–20% in test cases while enhancing the precision of fabricated components. Results will be disseminated through technical workshops at partner fabrication institutes and integrated into the program’s blueprint interpretation curriculum, fostering data-driven decision-making in industrial trades.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to further process ferrous and/or non-ferrous metal plates or shapes, and to manufacture and/or install products as interpreted through technical drawings. Includes instruction in trade tools, shop equipment, reading and interpreting blueprints, material handling, welding, thermal cutting, metallurgy, template pattern development, plate and structural fabrication, destructive and non-destructive testing, inspection, shipment preparation and fabrication installation.

abstract: This project seeks to address gaps in large-scale computational analysis of Norwegian linguistic diversity and literary evolution by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Norwegian dialects and historical texts present complex phonological, morphological, and syntactic variations that are challenging to systematically analyze with traditional methods due to the scale and multidimensionality of the data. The research will focus on two interrelated objectives: (1) modeling dialectal variation across modern Norwegian (Bokmål, Nynorsk, and regional dialects) using machine learning-driven phonetic and lexical analysis, and (2) tracing semantic and stylistic shifts in 19th- to 21st-century Norwegian literature through corpus linguistics and natural language processing (NLP). Computational workflows will integrate speech corpora (including the Nordic Dialect Corpus), digitized historical texts, and contemporary sources, applying transformer-based models for cross-dialect comparison and diachronic text analysis. HPC resources are essential for training custom tokenizers to handle orthographic variations in older texts, running parallelized acoustic analyses of dialect recordings, and processing multi-terabyte datasets with attention-based architectures. Expected outcomes include the first computational typology of Norwegian dialect boundaries, an open-access repository of annotated historical texts, and quantitative frameworks for detecting literary influences across eras. These resources will advance philological research, support language preservation efforts for endangered dialects, and enable robust NLP tools tailored to Norwegian’s linguistic specificity. By integrating computational methods with traditional humanities scholarship, this project aims to establish new interdisciplinary paradigms for studying lesser-resourced languages within the digital humanities.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Norwegian language and related dialects. Includes instruction in philology; dialects; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This project seeks to characterize the structural organization of multisensory integration hubs in the mammalian thalamus, with a focus on resolving unresolved synaptic connectivity patterns that underlie neurological disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. A critical barrier in mapping these circuits lies in analyzing the ultrastructure of thalamic nuclei at synaptic resolution across large tissue volumes—a task requiring petabyte-scale imaging datasets from serial electron microscopy and correlated light-electron microscopy. Current open-source tools for automated reconstruction of neural circuits are insufficiently optimized for the anisotropic resolution and staining variability inherent to thalamic datasets, necessitating custom computational pipelines. We request high-performance computing (HPC) resources to deploy a hybrid workflow combining GPU-accelerated deep learning for voxel-wise synapse classification, distributed CPU-based morphological tracing of long-range axonal projections, and graph-theoretical analysis of synaptic motifs. The proposed pipeline will process 50 TB of initial imaging data (3,000 coronal sections from murine thalamus), leveraging SLURM-managed parallelization for iterative model training and multi-scale registration. Validation will involve ground-truth comparison with manual reconstructions from the anterior pulvinar nucleus. This resource-intensive approach is expected to 1) generate the first connectome of thalamocortical circuits involved in multisensory processing, 2) identify pathognomonic alterations in synaptic bouton distribution in a transgenic ASD mouse model, and 3) release open-access thalamus-specific segmentation models to address a critical gap in neuroanatomical toolkits. Outcomes will directly inform mechanistic studies of sensory processing deficits and provide a computational framework for ultrastructural analysis of subcortical regions. The project’s scale—processing datasets orders of magnitude larger than existing thalamic connectomics efforts—is unfeasible without dedicated HPC infrastructure for memory-intensive graph computations and teravoxel image stitching.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the structure of the central and peripheral nervous system in vertebrates or the nervous system of invertebrates. Includes instruction in cellular and circuit anatomy, mapping of neuronal pathways, anatomical distribution and mapping of neuronal signaling molecules and their receptors, and the anatomical basis of central nervous system diseases and disorders.

abstract: Effective resource allocation in research administration is critical yet challenged by the dynamic interplay of financial, ethical, and operational constraints in large-scale projects. This project seeks to address inefficiencies in allocating personnel, funding, and infrastructure by developing a computational framework that integrates predictive analytics with ethical and regulatory considerations. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will construct agent-based models to simulate project workflows under varying grant conditions, compliance requirements, and team structures. Machine learning algorithms, trained on historical data from NIH grants, clinical trial registries, and institutional financial reports, will identify patterns linking resource allocation strategies to project outcomes. The models will incorporate bioethical principles and regulatory benchmarks to evaluate compliance risks alongside financial viability. HPC capabilities are essential for processing multi-terabyte datasets and running millions of simulation iterations to explore optimal strategies in diverse scenarios. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source platform enabling administrators to visualize trade-offs between cost, timelines, and regulatory adherence, thereby enhancing strategic decision-making. This work bridges gaps in computational approaches to research administration, offering empirically validated tools to reduce cost overruns and ethical compliance failures in academic and clinical research settings. The project aligns with the program’s focus on advancing leadership through innovative management strategies, directly contributing to improved governance of multidisciplinary research enterprises.
cip_definition: A program designed to prepare formally trained, advanced-level personnel for research administration leadership positions at colleges and universities, government agencies, hospitals, nonprofit agencies, and in industry. Includes instruction in bioethics, biostatistics, ethical, legal and regulatory consideration in clinical investigation, financial analysis, grant writing, managing and monitoring clinical trials, project management, strategic planning, and team building.

abstract: Pediatric infectious diseases present unique challenges due to the dynamic interplay between evolving pathogens, developmental immune responses, and variable drug pharmacokinetics in children. Current clinical models often fail to account for the heterogeneity of pediatric populations, particularly in cases involving complex host conditions, antimicrobial resistance, or rare pathogens, leading to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop predictive, patient-specific models for optimizing treatment strategies in pediatric infections. We propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating host multi-omics data (genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic), pathogen genomes, and longitudinal clinical data from a diverse cohort of 1,500 pediatric patients with severe or recurrent infections. Machine learning algorithms will identify biomarkers associated with treatment failure or adverse drug reactions, while agent-based models will simulate host-pathogen interactions across developmental stages to predict disease trajectories. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) models, parameterized using pediatric physiological data, will evaluate drug efficacy and toxicity thresholds in virtual patient cohorts. These models will be validated against real-world clinical outcomes from partner children’s hospitals. HPC resources are critical for processing terabyte-scale datasets, training deep neural networks, and executing parallelized simulations across thousands of parameter combinations. Expected outcomes include predictive tools to guide antibiotic selection, dosing adjustments, and immunomodulatory interventions in complex cases, reducing trial-and-error prescribing. The project will also generate open-access computational workflows for pediatric infectious disease research, addressing a critical gap in age-specific therapeutic development. By bridging clinical data with scalable computational modeling, this work aims to improve survival rates, mitigate long-term complications, and establish a paradigm for precision medicine in pediatric infectious diseases.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of infectious diseases in children; and to effect a better outcome for pediatric infections with complicated courses, underlying diseases that predispose to unusual or severe infections, unclear diagnoses, uncommon diseases, and complex or investigational treatments.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop predictive models of hemodynamic instability during minimally invasive cardiovascular procedures, such as transcatheter aortic valve replacements (TAVR) or coronary angioplasties. Current clinical practice relies on static imaging and empirical thresholds to guide device selection and procedural planning, which often fails to account for dynamic, patient-specific biomechanical interactions. These limitations contribute to post-procedural complications, including paravalvular leaks or stent malpositioning. To address this, we propose a computational framework integrating real-time fluoroscopic imaging data with finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to simulate device-tissue interactions under physiologically accurate flow conditions. The research will utilize anonymized patient datasets (CT/MRI angiograms, intraoperative pressure tracings) to construct 3D cardiovascular geometries, which will be parameterized for material properties and boundary conditions. HPC resources will enable parallelized simulations across a range of physiological states (rest, exercise, arrhythmia) and device configurations, optimizing computational efficiency for near-real-time clinical applicability. Machine learning techniques will be applied to reduce model complexity by identifying key predictors of procedural success from simulation outputs. Expected outcomes include validated predictive algorithms for hemodynamic instability, which could inform intraoperative decision-making and pre-procedural planning tools. This work bridges gaps in cardiovascular technology by advancing patient-specific modeling beyond traditional imaging, offering a novel computational lens to refine device deployment strategies. Success would directly enhance the precision of cardiovascular technologists' workflows, reducing complication rates and improving long-term outcomes for patients undergoing structural heart interventions. The scalability of this approach could further support the development of adaptive training simulators for cardiovascular technologists, integrating biomechanical feedback into educational platforms.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform invasive, noninvasive, and peripheral examinations of the cardiovascular system at the request of physicians to aid in diagnoses and therapeutic treatments. Includes instruction in reviewing and recording patient histories and clinical data, patient care, investigative and examination procedures, diagnostic procedures, data analysis and documentation, physician consultation, equipment operation and monitoring, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in the computational analysis of understudied East Asian languages, with a focus on non-Sinitic and minority languages of the Tibeto-Burman, Tungusic, and Japonic families. These languages, many of which are endangered or lack comprehensive digital corpora, exhibit complex morphosyntactic structures and dialectal variations that challenge conventional linguistic analysis. The primary research problem lies in the inadequacy of existing computational tools—often optimized for widely spoken languages like Mandarin or Japanese—to parse, model, or classify lesser-documented languages with divergent grammatical features. To overcome these limitations, the project will employ deep learning architectures, including transformer-based models and graph neural networks, to analyze phonetic, syntactic, and semantic patterns across multimodal datasets comprising historical texts, spoken narratives, and dialect recordings. HPC resources will enable large-scale parallel processing of these heterogeneous datasets, training models to identify cross-linguistic typological markers and reconstruct proto-language features. Additionally, the project will develop a federated corpus platform to aggregate and annotate fragmented linguistic materials from archival sources and fieldwork recordings, utilizing distributed computing for real-time collaborative annotation. Expected outcomes include (1) novel computational frameworks for low-resource language analysis, (2) empirically grounded insights into language contact phenomena in premodern East Asia, and (3) open-access tools for phonetic alignment and morphological segmentation tailored to non-Sinitic languages. By advancing methodologies for computationally modeling linguistic diversity, this work will directly support preservation efforts for endangered languages while providing humanities scholars with scalable analytical resources to interrogate historical language change and cultural exchange across East Asia.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: East Asian Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in East Asian languages, literatures, and linguistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding spatial and temporal population dynamics affecting public health infrastructure planning in aging populations. While demographic shifts are well-documented at macro scales, localized projections integrating real-time migration, mortality, and fertility data remain computationally constrained, limiting actionable insights for policymakers. We propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to model subnational population changes at unprecedented granularity (census tract level) across a 20-year horizon, combining agent-based microsimulation with Bayesian hierarchical spatial-temporal models. The research will integrate multi-source data, including U.S. Census microdata, Medicare utilization records, and georeferenced vital statistics, to simulate individual life-course trajectories while accounting for spatial dependencies and uncertainty propagation. Computational challenges include parallel processing of 100+ million agent interactions per simulation year, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation for high-dimensional spatial models, and real-time visualization of uncertainty metrics through GPU-accelerated geospatial analytics. The HPC environment is essential for scaling ensemble simulations across parameter spaces, reducing runtime from estimated 18 months on local clusters to 6 weeks via distributed memory parallelism and optimized memory handling for terabyte-scale demographic datasets. Expected outcomes include (1) open-source tools for adaptive demographic forecasting under policy scenarios, (2) vulnerability indices identifying regions at risk of healthcare infrastructure mismatches, and (3) validation frameworks comparing model projections against emerging migration patterns observed in the 2020s post-pandemic era. This work directly supports evidence-based decision-making for hospital capacity planning, geriatric service allocation, and regional workforce development strategies, while advancing methodological integration of demographic microsimulation with spatially explicit uncertainty quantification.
detailed_field: Sociology, demography, and population studies nec
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the practical application of demographic methods and materials for decision-making in business, education, health, and government. Includes instruction in statistics, research methods, geographic information systems, and demographic methods and techniques.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven predictive analytics framework to optimize credentialing and privileging workflows in healthcare institutions, addressing inefficiencies in Medical Staff Services (MSS) operations. Traditional credentialing processes are labor-intensive, prone to delays, and vulnerable to human error, creating bottlenecks that impact healthcare workforce readiness and institutional compliance. To overcome these challenges, we propose a computational approach integrating natural language processing (NLP) and graph neural networks (GNNs) to automate the extraction, validation, and risk assessment of practitioner credentials from heterogeneous data sources (e.g., licensure records, malpractice claims, peer references). High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for training large-scale language models on sensitive, unstructured text data (CVs, accreditation documents, legal transcripts) and constructing dynamic knowledge graphs mapping practitioner competencies, institutional requirements, and regulatory constraints. The pipeline will include federated learning to preserve data privacy across collaborating healthcare systems while enabling model refinement. Anticipated outcomes include a real-time decision support tool that reduces credentialing cycle times by ≥40%, identifies high-risk privileging scenarios with >90% precision, and dynamically aligns staffing resources with evolving care standards. By leveraging HPC to process multi-modal datasets at scale, this work bridges gaps between healthcare administration, regulatory informatics, and computational ethics—advancing a novel, technology-driven paradigm for MSS operations. The resulting open-source framework will be validated against retrospective data from three academic medical centers, with benchmarks shared publicly to inform standards for AI-augmented healthcare workforce management.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform credentialing, privileging, personnel management, and accreditation compliance services for hospitals and other health care facilities and organizations. Includes instruction in medical staff organization and management, medical terminology, credentialing and re-credentialing, health care accreditation and regulatory standards, health care law, meeting and negotiation management, and office information systems management.

abstract: This research project seeks to investigate the optimization of supply chain resilience strategies under climate-induced disruptions through computational economic modeling, addressing a critical gap in traditional managerial economics frameworks. While firms increasingly face climate-related risks, existing models often fail to capture the dynamic interdependencies between economic decision-making, resource allocation, and stochastic environmental shocks. The project will develop an agent-based simulation platform to model multi-tier supply networks under varying climate scenarios, integrating firm-level cost-benefit analyses with macroeconomic shock propagation. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute large-scale parallel simulations that incorporate heterogeneous agent behaviors, non-linear price adjustments, and probabilistic disruption events across geographies and industries. The computational framework will leverage econometric calibration using historical supply chain disruption data and climate projection datasets, enabling validation against real-world cases. Expected outcomes include identifying economically viable adaptation strategies—such as dynamic inventory buffering, supplier diversification thresholds, and contingency pricing mechanisms—that balance short-term efficiency with long-term resilience. The project will further produce sensitivity analyses quantifying how regulatory environments and market competition modulate the effectiveness of resilience investments. By bridging environmental uncertainty modeling with microeconomic decision theory, this research aims to advance managerial economics methodologies while providing actionable insights for firms navigating climate volatility. The HPC component directly supports the iterative optimization of agent-based parameters and high-dimensional scenario testing, which are computationally intractable with conventional infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of economics principles to the analysis of the organization and operation of business enterprises. Includes instruction in monetary theory, banking and financial systems, theory of competition, pricing theory, wage and salary/incentive theory, analysis of markets, and applications of econometrics and quantitative methods to the study of particular businesses and business problems.

abstract: Brewing science faces significant challenges in optimizing fermentation processes, which are central to product consistency, flavor profile development, and operational efficiency. Traditional experimental approaches to strain selection, metabolic pathway analysis, and process parameter tuning are time-intensive and limited in their ability to resolve the complex interplay of microbial dynamics, biochemical reactions, and environmental variables. This project proposes a computational framework to model and simulate yeast metabolism and microbial interactions during fermentation at an unprecedented resolution. Leveraging genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and non-Saccharomyces species, we will integrate multi-omics data (transcriptomics, metabolomics) with dynamic fluid dynamics simulations to predict metabolic fluxes, substrate utilization, and byproduct formation under varying brewing conditions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to handle the computational load of these multi-scale simulations, which involve solving systems of differential equations across spatial and temporal scales, from intracellular enzyme kinetics to vessel-scale nutrient gradients. Machine learning techniques will further refine parameter optimization, enabling rapid iteration of strain engineering targets and process variables. Expected outcomes include identifying yeast strain combinations and fermentation protocols that minimize off-flavor compounds, enhance ethanol yield, and improve temperature resilience. This work will advance precision brewing methodologies, reduce production waste, and provide a transferable computational toolkit for microbial community management in fermentation-dependent industries. By bridging systems biology with brewing technology, the project aligns with the agricultural sciences' mandate to innovate food production systems while addressing industry demands for scalability and sustainability.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the business, science, and technology of beer brewing operations. Includes instruction in biology, biochemistry, brewing, entrepreneurship, fermentation, malting, marketing, microbiology, quality control, and sanitation.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational workflows to address the growing demands of high-resolution, real-time media processing in photographic and film/video production. Current workflows struggle to efficiently manage ultra-high-definition (8K+) video streams, multi-camera synthetic environments, and AI-driven postproduction tasks, which require rapid processing of large datasets. The research problem centers on overcoming latency, storage bottlenecks, and computational limitations that hinder creative flexibility and technical precision in time-sensitive production environments. To address this, the project proposes leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to parallelize and optimize three core processes: (1) real-time rendering of complex visual effects (VFX) using GPU-accelerated ray tracing, (2) machine learning (ML)-based restoration of archival film via neural networks trained on degraded/restored frame pairs, and (3) dynamic simulation of virtual production environments for previsualization. Computational methods will include distributed processing of raw video data across nodes, in-memory caching for frame-sequential tasks, and hybrid CPU/GPU pipelines for ML inference. The project will utilize containerized workflows to ensure compatibility with industry-standard software (e.g., DaVinci Resolve, Unreal Engine). Expected outcomes include a scalable framework for processing 8K footage at sub-frame latency, a publicly accessible dataset of film degradation patterns paired with ML restoration models, and performance benchmarks for virtual production simulations. This work will directly enhance pedagogical resources by enabling student-led research in computational cinematography while providing industry practitioners with open-source tools to reduce postproduction timelines. The requested HPC allocation is critical to handling petascale visual data and achieving the fine-grained parallelism required for these computationally intensive tasks, which cannot feasibly be executed on local workstations.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the operation and maintenance of camera and lighting equipment and the production of finished still, video, and film products under the supervision of photographers, directors, and editors. Includes instruction in equipment setup and maintenance; lighting; power supplies; studio and film set tasks such as camera operator, grip, and best boy; plate and negative handling and development; laboratory procedures; and digital software applications.

abstract: The increasing complexity of drug discovery and toxicological risk assessment demands advanced computational tools to predict adverse outcomes with higher accuracy. A critical challenge in pharmacology is understanding the mechanistic basis of organ-specific toxicity, particularly hepatotoxicity, which remains a leading cause of drug attrition in clinical trials. Current in vitro and in silico models often fail to capture the dynamic interplay between drug metabolism, cellular stress pathways, and tissue-level responses. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing a multi-scale computational framework integrating physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, agent-based simulations of hepatic cellular networks, and machine learning-driven toxicity prediction. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to parameterize PBPK models using population-level pharmacokinetic data, simulate heterogeneous cell populations under varying drug exposures, and train deep neural networks on high-dimensional toxicogenomics datasets. The computational workflow will leverage GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics to model drug-enzyme interactions (e.g., cytochrome P450 isoforms) and parallelized Monte Carlo methods to quantify uncertainty in toxicity thresholds. Expected outcomes include: (1) predictive models for hepatotoxicity risk stratification across diverse chemical classes, (2) mechanistic insights into metabolic activation pathways contributing to liver injury, and (3) a publicly accessible database of simulated toxicity trajectories for 200+ known hepatotoxicants. By bridging gaps between subcellular drug metabolism and tissue-level adverse outcomes, this work will enhance preclinical safety evaluation and inform the design of safer therapeutics. The requested HPC allocation will enable large-scale parameter sweeps (>10,000 CPU-core hours), storage of petabyte-scale simulation outputs, and real-time analytics through distributed computing pipelines, which are computationally intractable with standard laboratory infrastructure.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in pharmacology and toxicology, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to integrate computational modeling and simulation into the creation and analysis of complex metal artworks, addressing the challenge of optimizing material behavior, structural integrity, and aesthetic outcomes in advanced metalworking processes. Traditional methods in metal arts—such as casting, welding, and electroforming—rely heavily on iterative physical experimentation, which is time-intensive, resource-heavy, and limited in its ability to predict nuanced material interactions. By leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we aim to develop predictive models for thermomechanical stresses during casting, electrochemical dynamics in anodizing and electroforming, and microstructural evolution in alloys under varying fabrication conditions. These simulations will employ finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning algorithms trained on empirical data from studio experiments. The project also explores generative design algorithms to iteratively refine 3D-printed metal sculptures, balancing geometric complexity with manufacturability constraints. Outcomes will include a library of open-source computational tools tailored to metal arts practitioners, enabling data-driven decision-making in studio practice. Additionally, the research will produce a series of hybrid digital-physical artworks that demonstrate the integration of computational insights with traditional craftsmanship. By bridging gaps between material science, computational engineering, and artistic practice, this work aims to expand the technical and expressive possibilities of metal arts while reducing material waste and energy consumption. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling large-scale simulations of multi-physics processes and training neural networks on high-resolution imaging data of metal surfaces. This interdisciplinary approach positions computational methods as a transformative force in visual arts pedagogy and creative practice, fostering new dialogues between technology and handcrafted materiality.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the development of individual artistic expression and technical skills necessary for fabricating refined metal works. Includes instruction in aesthetics, anodizing, art history, casting, design, electroforming, enameling, metalsmithing, sculpture, two and three-dimensional design, wax carving, and welding.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the study of dynamic financial decision-making in households facing economic volatility, a core concern within Family Resource Management Studies. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how families adapt resource allocation strategies under stressors such as income instability, unexpected expenses, or shifting access to public support systems. Existing models often rely on static or simplified assumptions about household behavior, limiting their ability to capture the nonlinear interactions between financial constraints, psychological factors, and policy interventions. To overcome these limitations, the project employs a multi-agent simulation framework that integrates behavioral economics principles, real-world financial datasets, and stochastic modeling of income and expense shocks. Each agent represents a household with heterogeneous attributes, including savings rates, debt profiles, risk tolerance, and awareness of public assistance programs. The computational approach requires iterative optimization to simulate millions of potential decision pathways across diverse demographic and economic scenarios, necessitating parallelized processing for parameter calibration and sensitivity analysis. By incorporating machine learning techniques to identify patterns in adaptive financial behaviors, the model aims to predict which combinations of household characteristics and external conditions lead to sustainable resource management versus financial distress. Expected outcomes include a scalable computational toolkit for simulating policy impacts on household resilience, evidence-based insights into the effectiveness of targeted financial literacy interventions, and publicly accessible synthetic datasets reflecting complex decision-making dynamics. The results will directly inform the design of adaptive financial counseling frameworks and contribute to methodological innovation in non-STEM applications of HPC, demonstrating the transformative potential of computational social science in family resource management research.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the design and implementation of policies and processes contributing to successful individual and family resource management. Includes instruction in financial goal-setting and strategies; household income, assets, and debt management; preventing and resolving financial difficulties; and the use of relevant public resources.

abstract: This project seeks to advance fire prevention and safety planning in complex urban environments through high-fidelity computational modeling of fire spread dynamics and human evacuation behavior. Traditional fire risk assessments often rely on simplified models that inadequately capture the interplay between building geometries, ventilation systems, combustible materials, and crowd movement during emergencies. This limitation hinders the development of optimized safety protocols for high-density structures such as mixed-use towers, underground transit hubs, and heritage buildings with unique architectural constraints. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we propose to develop a coupled simulation framework integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for fire-smoke propagation and agent-based modeling (ABM) for occupant egress. The CFD component will employ large-eddy simulations to resolve turbulent combustion and toxic plume dispersion at sub-meter scales across multi-story domains, while the ABM module will incorporate cognitive decision-making algorithms calibrated to behavioral studies of evacuees under sensory impairment. A key innovation lies in dynamically linking these models to enable real-time feedback between fire conditions and occupant movement, a computationally intensive process requiring parallelized solvers and distributed memory architectures. The project will validate simulations against full-scale experimental fire datasets and historical incident reports, then apply the framework to case studies of high-risk urban infrastructure. Anticipated outcomes include predictive tools for identifying latent vulnerabilities in emergency evacuation routes, data-driven recommendations for staggered evacuation protocols, and evidence-based guidelines for retrofitting legacy structures with adaptive smoke control systems. By addressing critical gaps in scenario-specific fire safety planning, this work aims to reduce preventable casualties and economic losses while informing next-generation building codes tailored to evolving urban design challenges.
cip_definition: A program focusing on the application of fire science and technology to problems of reducing fire risk, limiting loss, supervising substance removal, conducting safety inspections and investigations, and advising on matters of safety procedures and fire prevention policy. Includes instruction in fire behavior, fire simulation, structural risk assessment, materials analysis, detection and suppression systems, smoke management, supply and evacuation, public education, legal aspects of fire prevention, and related research and communications methods.

abstract: The poultry industry faces critical challenges in optimizing production efficiency, disease resistance, and sustainability while meeting growing global protein demands. Current limitations in understanding the complex interactions between avian genetics, gut microbiota dynamics, and nutritional interventions hinder progress. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address these challenges through advanced genomic and microbiomic modeling. We propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of poultry breeds with machine learning-driven analyses of gut microbial ecosystems. Using whole-genome sequencing data from broiler and layer populations, we will identify genetic markers linked to disease resilience and feed efficiency. Concurrently, metagenomic datasets from poultry gut microbiomes will be analyzed to model microbial community responses to dietary additives and environmental stressors. These datasets will inform agent-based simulations of host-microbiome interactions under varying nutritional regimes. The computational workflow requires large-scale parallel processing for alignment of terabase-scale sequencing data, Bayesian hierarchical modeling of genotype-phenotype associations, and dynamic flux balance analysis of microbial metabolic networks. By coupling these approaches, we aim to predict optimal genetic selection criteria and feed formulations that maximize growth performance while reducing antibiotic dependence. The HPC infrastructure is essential for managing the project's data volume (>500 TB raw sequencing data), complex model integration, and iterative simulations across biological scales. Expected outcomes include predictive models for precision poultry nutrition, candidate genes for selective breeding programs, and a computational toolkit for optimizing hatchery environments. This work will provide transformative insights into avian systems biology, directly supporting the development of sustainable poultry production strategies that align with global food security priorities.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of biological and chemical principles to the production and management of poultry animals and the production and handling of poultry products. Includes instruction in avian sciences, nutrition sciences, food science and technology, biochemistry, hatchery design, and related aspects of human and animal health and safety.

abstract: Aerospace medicine faces critical challenges in understanding and mitigating the physiological and psychological stressors experienced by crew members and passengers during prolonged air and space missions. Extended exposure to microgravity, radiation, circadian disruption, and confined environments contributes to multisystem degradation, including cardiovascular deconditioning, muscle atrophy, neurocognitive deficits, and immune dysfunction. Current countermeasures remain insufficient for long-duration missions, such as crewed Mars expeditions, necessitating advanced predictive models to optimize interventions. This project proposes a computational physiology framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate integrated human responses to aerospace environments and evaluate targeted countermeasures. Multiscale biomechanical models will couple cardiovascular fluid dynamics, musculoskeletal adaptations, and neural control systems under microgravity conditions, informed by astronaut biometric data from orbital missions. Concurrently, machine learning algorithms will analyze multi-omics datasets (genomic, proteomic, metabolomic) to identify biomarkers of resilience and predict individualized health risks. HPC resources are essential for resolving the spatiotemporal complexity of whole-body simulations, enabling real-time modeling of autonomic regulation during extravehicular activities and high-G maneuvers. The computational pipeline will also test virtual interventions, including optimized exercise protocols, artificial gravity profiles, and pharmacological strategies, through probabilistic risk assessment workflows. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms to personalize countermeasure regimens, reduce mission-critical health failures, and inform next-generation vehicle life-support systems. By bridging clinical data with systems-level computational models, this work aims to establish scalable frameworks for maintaining human performance in extreme environments, directly supporting the development of evidence-based medical standards for emerging commercial spaceflight and deep-space exploration programs.
cip_definition: Research focused on the health care of operating crews, support personnel, and passengers of air and space vehicles. Includes instruction in special conditions of physical and psychological stress, emergency medical procedures, adaptive systems and artificial environments. One of three general certificates in the area of preventive medicine.

abstract: Marine ecosystems are experiencing rapid environmental changes due to climate stressors, yet predicting species-specific responses and ecosystem-wide impacts remains a critical challenge. This project seeks to advance understanding of how ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation interact to reshape marine biodiversity and biogeochemical cycles, with a focus on pelagic and coastal ecosystems. We propose to develop a high-resolution, trait-based modeling framework integrating species physiological thresholds, planktonic community dynamics, and physical oceanographic processes. The computational approach combines large-scale biogeochemical simulations (using the Community Earth System Model) with individual-based models for key taxa, leveraging machine learning to parameterize metabolic responses from multi-omics datasets (metagenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic). High-performance computing resources are essential to resolve fine-scale spatiotemporal variability in coastal upwelling systems and to conduct ensemble simulations across IPCC climate scenarios. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of tipping points in microbial community structure linked to carbon export efficiency, (2) probabilistic projections of habitat compression for commercially important fish species, and (3) quantification of synergistic effects between multiple stressors on coral reef resilience. The generated datasets will be synthesized into an open-access portal supporting regional fisheries management and marine protected area design. By bridging molecular-scale biological processes with ecosystem-level dynamics, this work will provide a critical computational toolkit for anticipating climate-driven regime shifts in ocean environments.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the ecology and behavior of microbes, plants, and animals inhabiting oceans, coastal waters, and saltwater wetlands and their interactions with the physical environment. Includes instruction in chemical, physical, and geological oceanography; molecular, cellular, and biochemical studies; marine microbiology; marine botany; ichthyology; mammalogy; marine population dynamics and biodiversity; reproductive biology; studies of specific species, phyla, habitats, and ecosystems; marine paleocology and palentology; and applications to fields such as fisheries science and biotechnology.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the biomechanical mechanisms underpinning plant-parasitic nematode invasion of root systems, a process responsible for billions of dollars in annual agricultural losses. Current understanding of nematode root penetration focuses on biochemical interactions, leaving critical gaps in knowledge about the physical forces and structural adaptations enabling these organisms to breach plant tissues. We propose a computational study integrating high-resolution finite element analysis (FEA) and fluid-structure interaction (FSI) modeling to simulate the dynamic mechanical interplay between nematode stylets (spear-like mouthparts) and root cell walls under varying soil conditions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable 3D simulations of stylet kinematics, stress distribution during penetration, and the role of soil moisture gradients in modulating root tissue resistance. Multiscale models will parameterize stylet morphology from micro-CT scans of economically significant species (e.g., *Meloidogyne incognita*) and incorporate experimentally derived viscoelastic properties of root cells. The simulations will identify mechanical failure thresholds of plant tissues and optimize nematode attack strategies, revealing evolutionary adaptations that enhance parasitic efficiency. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework linking nematode morphometrics to invasion success, with applications in designing nematode-resistant crop architectures and biomimetic tools for precision agriculture. By bridging biomechanics and parasitology, this work establishes a novel computational paradigm for understanding physically driven host-pathogen interactions, offering translational insights distinct from conventional biochemical control approaches.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of nematode (roundworm) species and populations in respect of their life cycles, morphology, genetics, physiology, ecology, taxonomy, population dynamics, and environmental and economic impacts.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-fidelity computational framework to optimize additive manufacturing (AM) processes for advanced metallic alloys, addressing critical challenges in defect formation and microstructure control. Current AM techniques suffer from inconsistent mechanical properties due to rapid, non-uniform thermal gradients and residual stresses, which are difficult to predict using conventional modeling tools. To overcome these limitations, the proposed research will employ multi-physics simulations integrating thermal, fluid dynamics, and solid mechanics models to capture the complex interactions during laser-powder bed fusion. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve micron-scale melt pool dynamics, track phase transformations, and predict stress evolution across macroscale part geometries. A hybrid approach combining finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning-based surrogate models will be implemented to reduce computational costs while maintaining accuracy. The simulations will be validated against synchrotron X-ray imaging and electron backscatter diffraction data from collaborative experimental trials. Expected outcomes include a predictive toolset for optimizing laser parameters, scan strategies, and support structures to minimize defects such as porosity and cracking. This work will advance the fundamental understanding of process-structure-property relationships in AM, enabling the reliable production of high-performance components for aerospace and energy applications. The requested HPC allocation will support large-scale parametric studies (>10,000 core-hours) requiring parallelized solvers and distributed memory architectures to handle datasets exceeding 50 TB. By bridging simulation scales and accelerating process development, this project aims to reduce trial-and-error costs by 30-40% and establish open-source benchmarks for the AM research community.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in mechanical engineering-related technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the spatial and social dynamics of Reconstruction-era (1865–1877) migration patterns among formerly enslaved populations in the United States. Traditional historiography has relied on fragmented records—such as census data, Freedmen’s Bureau documents, and newspaper archives—to reconstruct these movements, but gaps and biases in source materials have limited comprehensive analysis. This research addresses these challenges by integrating computational methods, including geospatial mapping, network analysis, and probabilistic record linkage, to aggregate and analyze disparate datasets at scale. Using HPC capabilities, the project will process over 500,000 digitized records, including tax rolls, labor contracts, and correspondence, to model migration routes, kinship networks, and economic adaptations. Machine learning algorithms will assist in identifying patterns of displacement, resettlement, and community formation, while geospatial tools (e.g., GIS) will visualize interactions between migration flows and federal/state policies. The computational demands of cross-referencing heterogeneous data—requiring parallel processing, large-scale data storage, and high memory bandwidth—necessitate HPC infrastructure. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible interactive map and database documenting Reconstruction-era migration, shedding light on how emancipated individuals navigated post-war legal and social landscapes. This work will contribute to broader debates about race, agency, and citizenship in American history while demonstrating the transformative potential of computational methods in humanities research. By bridging quantitative scalability with qualitative depth, the project aims to set a methodological precedent for historical inquiries into marginalized populations.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the development of American society, culture, and institutions from the Pre-Columbian period to the present. Includes instruction in American historiography, American history sources and materials, historical research methods, and applications to the study of specific themes, issues, periods, and institutions.

abstract: The development of advanced polymeric materials with tailored properties for sustainable applications remains a critical challenge in plastics and polymer engineering. Current experimental approaches to optimize polymer formulations and processing parameters are time-intensive and lack the resolution to predict nanoscale interactions that govern macroscopic material behavior. This project seeks to address these limitations by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model polymer systems at multiple scales, enabling the rational design of materials with enhanced mechanical, thermal, and environmental performance. The research will focus on two interconnected objectives: (1) simulating polymerization kinetics and chain dynamics using molecular dynamics (MD) and coarse-grained Monte Carlo methods to predict molecular weight distributions and branching behavior, and (2) employing finite element analysis (FEA) to model polymer melt flow during extrusion and injection molding processes under varying thermal and shear conditions. These computational studies will be validated against experimental data from collaborator laboratories, including rheological measurements and spectroscopic characterization. The scale of simulations—involving systems with over 10^6 particles and multi-physics coupling—necessitates access to parallelized computing architectures and GPU-accelerated nodes. Expected outcomes include predictive frameworks for structure-process-property relationships in industrial polymers, with direct applications to biodegradable packaging materials and high-strength recyclable composites. By reducing trial-and-error prototyping, this work aims to accelerate the development of sustainable polymer technologies while minimizing resource consumption. The generated datasets and open-source simulation tools will be shared with the broader polymer engineering community to foster collaborative innovation in material science.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and other professionals engaged in developing and using industrial polymers. Includes instruction in the principles of macromolecular chemistry, polymerization and plastic manufacturing processes and equipment, design and operational testing procedures, equipment maintenance and repair procedures, safety procedures, applications to specific products, and report preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to analyze and model the acquisition of French grammatical structures among second language (L2) learners, with the goal of informing adaptive pedagogical strategies. A key challenge in teaching French as a foreign language lies in addressing persistent errors in complex grammatical areas such as verb conjugation, gender agreement, and syntactic negation. Traditional pedagogical assessments often lack the granularity to identify nuanced, learner-specific error patterns across diverse cohorts. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process multimodal datasets of learner interactions—including written assignments, speech recordings, and real-time classroom response data—from over 5,000 intermediate-level students. Natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will be optimized to annotate errors, classify their linguistic sources, and map developmental trajectories using transformer-based models. Concurrently, agent-based simulations will model the efficacy of different instructional interventions under varying learner profiles. The computational workload necessitates parallelized processing of text and audio data, large-scale parameter sweeps for simulation calibration, and training of ensemble models to predict error persistence. Expected outcomes include (1) a corpus of annotated learner errors with associated pedagogical recommendations, (2) evidence-based guidelines for personalizing grammar instruction based on learner cognition patterns, and (3) open-source tools for automated error detection integrated into teacher training modules. By elucidating the dynamics of French grammatical acquisition at unprecedented scale, this work aims to equip educators with data-driven strategies to reduce fossilized errors and accelerate proficiency. The project directly aligns with the program’s mission to advance French language teaching through innovative, empirically grounded methodologies.
cip_title: Teaching French as a Second or Foreign Language
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the principles and practice of teaching French to students who are not proficient in French or who do not speak, read, or write French, and prepares individuals to serve as teachers and administrators.

abstract: The increasing demand for high-integrity welded joints in advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure, and robotic automation requires precise control of welding processes under complex multi-physics conditions. However, traditional experimental methods and low-fidelity simulations struggle to resolve dynamic interactions between thermal gradients, phase transformations, residual stresses, and molten pool behavior at the spatiotemporal scales relevant to industrial applications. This project seeks to address these challenges through high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled modeling of arc welding processes, with a focus on optimizing parameter selection and predicting defect formation in multi-pass steel welds. A coupled computational framework will integrate finite element analysis (FEA) for heat transfer and stress evolution, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for melt pool dynamics, and machine learning (ML) for rapid parameter optimization. High-resolution simulations will capture microstructural changes during rapid solidification using CALPHAD-based phase prediction tools, while parallelized thermal-mechanical models will quantify distortion and residual stress accumulation across sequential weld passes. The HPC environment is critical for managing the computational intensity of 3D transient simulations with adaptive meshing, particularly when analyzing the effects of process variables (e.g., travel speed, current waveform) on defect susceptibility metrics like hot cracking indices. Validation will leverage experimental data from in-situ monitoring systems, including high-speed imaging and acoustic emission sensors. Expected outcomes include a predictive digital twin framework capable of reducing trial-and-error prototyping by 40-60% for complex joint configurations, as well as new insights into process-structure-property relationships for emerging wire-arc additive manufacturing applications. By enabling atomistic-to-macroscale simulations on timescales aligned with industrial R&D cycles, this work will directly support workforce training in computational welding engineering and advance the adoption of AI-driven process control systems in welding technology.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills to the design and engineering of welding and joining systems and the implementation of welding processes. Includes instruction in materials science; computer-aided design; welding design; welding processes; welding metallurgy; automation and robotics; and codes, inspections, testing, and quality assurance.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a multi-scale computational framework to optimize the design of advanced composite materials for high-performance manufacturing applications. A critical challenge in materials engineering lies in predicting how atomic-scale interactions and microstructural features collectively influence the macroscopic mechanical and thermal properties of composite systems, particularly those involving novel bonding interfaces or hybrid material phases. Traditional experimental approaches are resource-intensive and struggle to capture the coupled effects of processing variables, defect dynamics, and interfacial phenomena across spatial and temporal scales. We propose an integrated computational strategy combining density functional theory (DFT) simulations, phase-field modeling, and finite element analysis (FEA) to establish structure-property relationships in metal-ceramic and polymer-matrix composites. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of interfacial adhesion mechanisms, parallelized phase-field computations of microstructure evolution during processing, and stochastic FEA simulations assessing mechanical performance under operational loads. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify optimal processing parameters and material combinations from the multi-terabyte simulation datasets generated. This approach addresses critical gaps in predicting failure initiation at bonded interfaces and quantifying the effects of residual stresses from manufacturing. Successful implementation will yield validated predictive models for designing composites with tailored strength-to-weight ratios, thermal stability, and damage tolerance, directly supporting applications in sustainable infrastructure and energy-efficient manufacturing systems. The requested computing resources are essential for handling the memory-intensive quantum mechanical calculations, multi-physics coupling across scales, and data-driven optimization workflows inherent to this research. Outcomes will advance computational materials design methodologies while providing open-access datasets to accelerate innovation in industrial materials development.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and materials science principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of materials and related processes used in manufacturing in a wide variety of settings; the synthesis of new industrial materials, including marrying and bonding composites; analysis of materials requirements and specifications; and related problems of system design dependent on materials factors.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the computational analysis of legal texts, policies, and historical records central to Tribal and Indigenous law. The research addresses a critical gap in legal scholarship: the lack of scalable, data-driven methods to analyze the complex interplay between federal Indian law, tribal legal systems, and Indigenous rights frameworks. Traditional legal research methods, which rely heavily on manual case review and qualitative interpretation, struggle to systematically map the evolution of legal doctrines, identify patterns in judicial decision-making, or trace the sociolegal impacts of colonial legal structures on Indigenous communities. To address this, the project proposes an interdisciplinary computational approach combining natural language processing (NLP), network analysis, and machine learning (ML) to process large corpora of legal documents, treaties, court opinions, and tribal codes. Key objectives include developing custom NLP pipelines to extract relational data (e.g., citations, jurisdictional overlaps, treaty violations) and training ML models to detect latent biases or inconsistencies in judicial reasoning across federal-tribal legal interfaces. HPC resources are essential for handling the scale and complexity of datasets, which span centuries of legal texts and multilingual Indigenous language materials requiring advanced preprocessing. Anticipated outcomes include (1) an open-access computational toolkit for legal scholars and tribal policymakers to analyze precedent networks and policy impacts, (2) data visualizations illuminating systemic disparities in federal-tribal case law, and (3) a foundational dataset for comparative studies on Indigenous rights recognition. By integrating computational rigor with critical legal theory, this work aims to empower Tribal nations with evidence-based strategies for legal advocacy and policy reform while establishing a methodological precedent for computational legal studies in underrepresented juridical traditions.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law, policies, and regulations affecting federal Indian law, tribal law and policy, and Indigenous peoples' human rights.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model the dynamics of labor negotiation processes in industries undergoing rapid automation and AI integration. While traditional labor-management frameworks emphasize static variables such as wages and benefits, emerging challenges—such as algorithmic scheduling, gig work platforms, and AI-driven productivity monitoring—introduce complex, dynamic interdependencies that defy conventional analytical methods. The research problem centers on quantifying how these technological shifts alter power asymmetries between workers and employers during collective bargaining, particularly in sectors like logistics, healthcare, and manufacturing. Using agent-based modeling (ABM), we will simulate negotiation scenarios under varying technological, economic, and policy conditions. Computational agents will represent workers, unions, employers, and regulatory bodies, each programmed with adaptive decision-making algorithms informed by real-world labor dispute datasets and behavioral economics principles. The HPC environment will enable large-scale parallel simulations to explore "what-if" scenarios, such as the impact of universal basic income policies on strike behaviors or the role of predictive analytics in preempting grievances. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify emergent patterns in negotiation outcomes, including tipping points for worker mobilization or management concession strategies. Expected outcomes include a scalable computational framework to forecast labor relations risks in technologically disrupted industries, as well as policy recommendations for balancing innovation with equitable labor practices. By integrating computational social science with industrial relations theory, this project addresses a critical gap in understanding how digital transformation redefines workplace governance. The results will provide stakeholders with evidence-based tools to navigate contentious labor issues in an era of accelerating technological change.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on employee-management interactions and the management of issues and disputes regarding working conditions and worker benefit packages, and that may prepare individuals to function as labor or personnel relations specialists. Includes instruction in labor history, policies and strategies of the labor movement, union organization, labor-management negotiation, labor law and contract interpretation, labor economics, welfare and benefit packages, grievance procedures, and labor policy studies.

abstract: This research project seeks to address the growing complexity of systemic risk propagation in global financial networks, driven by the rapid evolution of decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystems and escalating geopolitical volatility. Traditional models of international financial stability struggle to capture the nonlinear interactions between centralized banking systems, cross-border payment infrastructures, and algorithmically driven DeFi markets, particularly under stress scenarios involving sanctions, supply chain disruptions, or currency weaponization. The core computational challenge lies in modeling multi-layered financial networks with real-time adaptive agents, where high-frequency cross-border payment data, smart contract interactions, and geopolitical event feeds must be processed simultaneously. To overcome these limitations, we propose developing a hybrid simulation framework combining dynamic network analysis, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and event-driven computational storytelling. The high-performance computing (HPC) component will enable parallelized scenario testing across distributed ledger architectures, foreign exchange (FX) liquidity pools, and central bank digital currency (CBDC) prototypes at scale. Key computational requirements include GPU-accelerated agent training environments, in-memory processing of petabyte-scale transaction graphs, and stochastic optimization of crisis response pathways. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for identifying critical contagion thresholds in international payment systems, stress-testing frameworks for hybrid (traditional/DeFi) financial architectures, and policy simulations for multilateral currency swap line activation. By creating the first integrated computational model of geopolitical-DeFi-tradfi interdependencies, this research aims to provide central banks and international financial institutions with actionable insights for maintaining global financial stability in an era of fragmented monetary ecosystems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to manage international financial operations and related currency transactions. Includes instruction in international banking, international monetary and financial policy, money and capital markets, foreign exchange, risk analysis, and international cash flow operations.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the sociocultural dynamics of sports fandom as a driver of collective identity formation in digital spaces. While sports studies traditionally relies on qualitative and small-scale quantitative methods, the scale and complexity of modern fan interactions—spanning social media platforms, streaming services, and augmented reality applications—demand computational approaches to analyze multimodal, longitudinal datasets. The research focuses on three interrelated problems: (1) modeling the emergence of transnational fan communities around emerging sports leagues, (2) quantifying the interplay between real-world athletic performance and digital fan engagement metrics, and (3) identifying patterns of cultural hybridity in fan-created content across linguistic and geopolitical boundaries. Computational methods will include large-language model (LLM) fine-tuning for multilingual sentiment analysis of fan discourse, graph neural networks to map community evolution across platforms, and agent-based simulations to test hypotheses about information cascades in fan networks. The workflow integrates terabyte-scale datasets from proprietary sports analytics APIs, public social media archives, and digitized historical records of fandom practices. By establishing a pipeline for sports cultural analytics, this project aims to produce both theoretical insights into 21st-century collective identity formation and practical tools for understanding fan-driven economic ecosystems. Anticipated outcomes include the first longitudinal map of fan network topology across major emerging sports markets, a computational framework for predicting community fracture points during cultural controversies, and open-source tools for ethical sports big data analysis. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling memory-intensive graph computations, training domain-specific LLMs on sports discourse corpora, and running parallelized simulations of fan interaction scenarios at societally relevant scales.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the psychological, sociological, and historical aspects of sport and physical activity. Includes instruction in theory of sport, sport psychology, sport in American society, gender and race/ethnicity and sport, and sports history.

abstract: The construction industry faces persistent challenges in optimizing material efficiency, logistical coordination, and structural resilience while adhering to sustainability goals and evolving building codes. Traditional analytical methods often lack the resolution to model complex interactions between material properties, environmental stressors, and dynamic construction workflows. This project proposes the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to simulate multi-scale construction processes, integrating material science, supply chain dynamics, and structural mechanics. The research will employ finite element analysis (FEA) to model stress distributions in novel sustainable materials, such as carbon-reduced concrete composites, under varying climatic and load conditions. Concurrently, discrete event simulations will optimize site logistics and equipment allocation, incorporating real-world constraints like weather variability and supply chain disruptions. Machine learning algorithms will be trained on historical project data to predict risks in construction timelines and material performance, enabling proactive mitigation strategies. By leveraging HPC resources, these computationally intensive models will operate at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolutions, enabling simultaneous analysis of molecular-scale material behaviors and project-scale operational interactions. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for material selection under sustainability criteria, dynamic resource allocation protocols, and a digital twin platform for real-time project monitoring. This work will advance the integration of computational modeling into construction engineering technology, providing actionable insights to reduce waste, improve cost efficiency, and enhance structural longevity. The project’s computational outputs will be validated against physical experiments and case studies from ongoing collaborations with regional construction firms. By bridging gaps between theoretical models and practical construction workflows, this research aims to establish a replicable framework for data-driven decision-making in the industry, ultimately supporting the transition to resilient, low-carbon infrastructure systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers, engineering contractors and other professionals engaged in the construction of buildings and related structures. Includes instruction in basic structural engineering principles and construction techniques, building site inspection, site supervision, construction personnel supervision, plan and specification interpretation, supply logistics and procurement, applicable building codes, and report preparation.

abstract: Cybersecurity defense strategies increasingly rely on dynamic, data-driven policy frameworks to address evolving threats, yet existing approaches often lack the computational rigor to model complex, large-scale adversarial behaviors in real-world systems. This project seeks to bridge this gap by developing a high-fidelity simulation environment to evaluate the efficacy of cybersecurity policies under diverse threat scenarios, with a focus on resilience metrics and adaptive response protocols. The research problem centers on the absence of scalable, empirically validated models that capture the interdependencies between human decision-making, organizational infrastructure, and adversarial innovation in cyberspace.
